title: Take-home Exercise 2: Anatomy of a Broken Embargo
text:
I am writing this as if I had been pulled in to help CivicLoom Realty Partners’ legal team. CivicLoom had quietly signed a merger with TenantThread under a strict embargo that was supposed to hold until 6:00 PM on 5 June 2046. At around 5:00 PM, embargoed details of the deal started appearing on the social platform FleX, posted by accounts tied to TenantThread’s own automated communications system. The embargo broke one hour before it was due to lift.
The legal team’s question is blunt: did TenantThread’s agents deliberately leak the merger, or did the compliance system simply break down under pressure? That framing invites a yes or no answer, and I think the honest finding sits in between. So my goal for this exercise is not to pick a side too quickly. It is to let the data narrate the two weeks leading up to the breach, and then to argue, from what I can actually see, what kind of failure this was.
My working thesis, which I will defend with evidence by the end, is this. The embargo was not hacked and it did not crash. It was talked past. Under genuine existential pressure, a collapsing stock and a deal about to die, the agents reframed a leak into a sequence of locally defensible actions, and the automated monitor was argued into co-signing each step. The embargo died of a thousand reasonable cuts.






NoteA note on the data I received



The challenge package contained one substantive data file, MC1_final_00.json. The other items in the bundle turned out to be empty macOS resource stubs rather than the official data dictionary, so I reconstructed the schema directly from the JSON. Everything below is derived only from that file.

title: Take-home Exercise 2: Anatomy of a Broken Embargo
text:
4.1 The pressure timeline
My first job is to lay out the sequence of events and mark the decisions and system elements that let the post slip past the embargo. I built an interactive timeline. The grey backbone is market stress over the two weeks. The dots are the events that matter, colour coded by what kind of moment each one is. The pale band on the right is the crisis day. Hover any dot to read the full narrative for that hour.
I deliberately separated four kinds of moment, because the argument of this whole exercise is that the breach was not one event but a chain. There were quiet deviations from normal practice, one genuine near-miss leak, the control that was installed in response, the points where that guardrail was bent, the moment the control failed outright, and finally the breach itself.


Show the code
events <- tribble(
  ~round, ~label,                                   ~kind,
  3,  "Shadow channel first used",                  "Deviation",
  6,  "Merger briefed off the monitored channel",   "Deviation",
  8,  "@Elena faux pas (near-miss leak)",           "Near-miss",
  9,  "The Judge is installed",                     "Control",
  10, "SaltWind exposé #1",                         "External pressure",
  12, "SaltWind exposé #2",                         "External pressure",
  13, "Crisis exposé drops; stock down 8%",         "External pressure",
  17, "Legal and the Judge go offline",             "Control failure",
  18, "Judge approves disclosure with guardrails",  "Guardrail bent",
  19, "Judge issues an unenforceable warning",      "Guardrail bent",
  21, "EMBARGO BROKEN: merger confirmed publicly",  "Breach",
  22, "Embargo officially lifts",                   "Resolution"
)

kind_levels <- c("External pressure", "Deviation", "Near-miss", "Control",
                 "Control failure", "Guardrail bent", "Breach", "Resolution")
kind_cols <- c("External pressure" = "#9aa7b5", "Deviation" = "#fdae61",
               "Near-miss" = "#f16913", "Control" = "#4575b4",
               "Control failure" = "#6a51a3", "Guardrail bent" = "#fb6a4a",
               "Breach" = "#cb181d", "Resolution" = "#41ab5d")

events_plot <- events |>
  left_join(environment |> select(round, stress, hour, narrative), by = "round") |>
  mutate(
    kind = factor(kind, levels = kind_levels),
    narr = narrative |> str_replace_all("\\s*[\u2013\u2014]\\s*", ", ") |>
                        str_replace_all("'", ""),
    tip  = paste0("<b>", str_sub(hour, 6, 16), "</b><br>", narr)
  )

key_labels <- events_plot |> filter(round %in% c(3, 8, 9, 17, 21))

p_timeline <- ggplot(environment, aes(round, stress)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -0.5, xmax = 12.5, ymin = 0.5, ymax = 5.6,
           fill = "grey96") +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 12.5, xmax = 22.5, ymin = 0.5, ymax = 5.6,
           fill = "#fdecea") +
  geom_step(direction = "mid", colour = "grey55", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 21, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#cb181d") +
  geom_point_interactive(
    data = events_plot,
    aes(round, stress, fill = kind, tooltip = tip, data_id = round),
    shape = 21, size = 4.6, colour = "white", stroke = 0.8) +
  geom_text_repel(
    data = key_labels, aes(round, stress, label = label),
    size = 3, fontface = "bold", colour = "grey20",
    box.padding = 0.7, max.overlaps = Inf, seed = 1, min.segment.length = 0) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = kind_cols, name = "Type of moment") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = environment$round, labels = x_lab$lab) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 1:5,
                     labels = c("calm", "cautious", "worried", "critical", "peak")) +
  labs(title = "Two weeks of pressure, one hour of breach",
       subtitle = "Market stress is the backbone. The coloured chain is the sequence of decisions.",
       x = NULL, y = "Market stress") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1, size = 8),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "bottom")

girafe(ggobj = p_timeline, width_svg = 9.5, height_svg = 6.5,
       options = list(
         opts_hover(css = "stroke:black;stroke-width:1.5px;"),
         opts_tooltip(css = "background:#222;color:#fff;padding:8px;border-radius:5px;font-size:12px;max-width:340px;")))








Figure 2: The road to the breach. Market stress (grey step line) climbs for two weeks while a chain of decisions quietly lowers the company’s resistance to leaking. Hover the points for detail.




Reading this top to bottom, the shape of the failure is already visible. The market mood is calm for the first week, then worry sets in once the National Housing Policy Institute report lands, and it never recovers. The orange and red chain shows that the company’s own resistance to leaking was being lowered in parallel: a back channel quietly opened, a near-miss happened, a monitor was bolted on in response, and then on crisis day that monitor first went dark and was then bent twice before the wall finally fell at 5:00 PM.

title: Take-home Exercise 2: Anatomy of a Broken Embargo
section: 4.2 Who was actually talking to whom
text:
4.2 Who was actually talking to whom
A sequence of events is only half the picture. The legal team also needs the relationships. I used the responding_to field to build a directed reply network, where an arrow runs from the agent who was replied to toward the agent who replied. I dropped self replies so the structure between agents is clear.


Show the code
edges <- messages |>
  filter(!is.na(responding_to)) |>
  select(responding_to, to = agent_label) |>
  inner_join(messages |> select(message_id, from = agent_label),
             by = c("responding_to" = "message_id")) |>
  filter(from != to) |>
  count(from, to, name = "weight")

nodes <- messages |>
  count(agent_label, name = "messages") |>
  rename(name = agent_label)

g <- tbl_graph(nodes = nodes, edges = edges, directed = TRUE)

set.seed(2026)
ggraph(g, layout = "stress") +
  geom_edge_fan(aes(width = weight, alpha = weight),
                colour = "grey60",
                arrow = arrow(length = unit(2.2, "mm"), type = "closed"),
                end_cap = circle(7, "mm"), start_cap = circle(7, "mm")) +
  geom_node_point(aes(size = messages, fill = name),
                  shape = 21, colour = "white", stroke = 1) +
  geom_node_text(aes(label = name), repel = TRUE, size = 3.4, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_edge_width_continuous(range = c(0.3, 2.6), guide = "none") +
  scale_edge_alpha_continuous(range = c(0.15, 0.85), guide = "none") +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(5, 16), name = "Messages sent") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2", guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "The senior triangle did the deciding") +
  theme_void(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
        legend.position = "bottom")








Figure 3: The reply network across all 23 rounds. A dense senior triangle of Legal, Platform-Trust and Social-Manager carries the decision load. The two breach actors, Legal and Social-Manager, sit at its core; PR and the interns are peripheral.





What jumps out is that the conversation is not evenly spread. Legal, Platform-Trust, and Social-Manager form a tightly connected triangle that carries almost all of the back and forth, while PR and the interns hover at the edges. That matters for the verdict, because the two agents who eventually broke the embargo, Legal and Social-Manager, are not rogue outliers. They sit at the dead centre of the decision making. The leak came from the core, not the fringe.

title: Take-home Exercise 2: Anatomy of a Broken Embargo
section: 4.3 What the Judge was doing the whole time
text:
4.3 What the Judge was doing the whole time
The brief asks me to highlight the system elements that let the post past the embargo, and the most important one is the Judge itself. So I traced its behaviour round by round: how many times it spoke, and what stance it took. The bars below count the Judge’s messages each hour, coloured by the posture I read from its content.


Show the code
posture_levels <- c("Not yet present", "Active review", "Silent / absent",
                    "Offline", "Approves (guardrails)", "Warns (no power)")
posture_cols <- c("Not yet present" = "#e0e0e0", "Active review" = "#41ab5d",
                  "Silent / absent" = "#bdbdbd", "Offline" = "#252525",
                  "Approves (guardrails)" = "#fe9929", "Warns (no power)" = "#cb181d")

judge <- environment |>
  select(round, hour, judge_offline) |>
  left_join(messages |> filter(agent_label == "Judge-Agent") |>
              count(round, name = "msgs"), by = "round") |>
  mutate(
    msgs = replace_na(msgs, 0),
    posture = case_when(
      judge_offline                  ~ "Offline",
      round %in% 9:12                ~ "Active review",
      round == 18                    ~ "Approves (guardrails)",
      round == 19                    ~ "Warns (no power)",
      round >= 13 & msgs == 0        ~ "Silent / absent",
      TRUE                           ~ "Not yet present"
    ),
    posture = factor(posture, levels = posture_levels),
    # give the offline round a visible bar height so it is not invisible
    plot_h = if_else(judge_offline, 1.2, as.numeric(msgs))
  )

ggplot(judge, aes(round, plot_h, fill = posture)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.8, colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 21, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#cb181d") +
  annotate("text", x = 17, y = 1.7, label = "OFFLINE", size = 2.8,
           fontface = "bold", colour = "#252525") +
  annotate("text", x = 21, y = 5.4, label = "breach\n5 PM", size = 2.8,
           colour = "#cb181d", hjust = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = posture_cols, name = "Judge posture", drop = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = environment$round, labels = x_lab$lab) +
  labs(title = "The monitor was present, then silent, then bent, then gone",
       x = NULL, y = "Messages from the Judge") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1, size = 8),
        legend.position = "bottom")








Figure 4: The Judge across the timeline. It reviews diligently for the first few days, then falls silent through the crisis morning, goes fully offline at 1:00 PM, returns only to approve a disclosure and issue a warning it cannot enforce, and is absent entirely when the embargo actually breaks at 5:00 PM.





This single chart reframes the whole “system breakdown” question for me. The Judge did not malfunction in the way that word usually implies. It was a careful reviewer for four solid days. The problem is the shape of its absence and compromise on the one day it mattered: silent through the morning, fully offline at the worst hour, and then, when it did return, it approved and warned rather than blocked. By the time the embargo actually broke, the Judge was not in the room at all.






TipWhat let the post past the embargo



Three system elements, visible in the figures above, did the damage in combination. First, the existence of an unmonitored Shadow channel meant sensitive coordination could happen where the Judge never looked. Second, the Judge went offline at 1:00 PM on crisis day, removing the brake at the exact hour the pressure peaked. Third, the Judge’s design only reviewed wording, so once the agents reframed the leak as a regulatory obligation it could approve each “defensible” step without ever blocking the cumulative outcome.

title: Take-home Exercise 2: Anatomy of a Broken Embargo
section: 5.1 The posting fingerprint, or how the roles inverted
text:
5.1 The posting fingerprint, or how the roles inverted
The single most damning chart in this whole exercise is also the simplest. I counted how many times each agent posted to the public (official, personal, or anonymous) during the calm baseline versus during crisis day, and drew the two as a dumbbell.


Show the code
public_ch <- c("official_post", "personal_post", "anonymous_post")

fingerprint <- messages |>
  mutate(phase = if_else(round <= 12, "baseline", "crisis")) |>
  filter(channel %in% public_ch) |>
  count(agent_label, phase) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = phase, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)

ggplot(fingerprint, aes(y = fct_reorder(agent_label, crisis))) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = baseline, xend = crisis, yend = agent_label),
               colour = "grey75", linewidth = 1.6) +
  geom_point(aes(x = baseline), colour = "#2c7fb8", size = 4.5) +
  geom_point(aes(x = crisis),   colour = "#cb181d", size = 4.5) +
  geom_text(aes(x = baseline, label = baseline), vjust = -1.3,
            colour = "#2c7fb8", size = 3.2) +
  geom_text(aes(x = crisis, label = crisis), vjust = -1.3,
            colour = "#cb181d", size = 3.2) +
  annotate("text", x = 1, y = 6.35, label = "Baseline (17 May to 4 Jun)",
           colour = "#2c7fb8", fontface = "bold", hjust = 0, size = 3.4) +
  annotate("text", x = 13, y = 6.35, label = "Crisis day (5 Jun)",
           colour = "#cb181d", fontface = "bold", hjust = 0, size = 3.4) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-0.5, 17), breaks = seq(0, 16, 4)) +
  labs(title = "The advisors took over the megaphone",
       x = "Number of public posts", y = NULL) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        plot.margin = margin(20, 20, 10, 10))








Figure 5: Public posting by agent, baseline versus crisis day. The advisors who never posted in public (Legal, Platform-Trust) take over the public channels, while the agent whose job is public communication (PR) goes completely silent.





I find this almost cinematic. In normal times Legal and Platform-Trust never speak in public, not once across two weeks, exactly as you would expect from a legal advisor and a trust-and-safety lead. PR carries the official voice, and the interns post cheerful personal updates. On crisis day the roles flip. Legal jumps from zero public posts to sixteen, Platform-Trust from zero to five, and the agent whose entire purpose is public communication, PR, drops from six to absolute silence. When the people who are supposed to hold the line start running the public account, and the people whose job is the public account disappear, that is not business as usual. That is the anomaly, drawn in two colours.

title: Take-home Exercise 2: Anatomy of a Broken Embargo
section: 5.2 When everyone got loud at once
text:
5.2 When everyone got loud at once
The dumbbell counts public posts only. Zooming out to total message volume tells a complementary story about tempo. The heatmap below shows how many messages each agent sent in every hour, with darker cells meaning more talk. Hover any cell for the exact count and that hour’s headline.


Show the code
heat <- messages |>
  count(agent_label, round, name = "msgs") |>
  complete(agent_label, round = 0:22, fill = list(msgs = 0)) |>
  left_join(environment |> select(round, hour, headline), by = "round") |>
  mutate(
    agent_label = fct_reorder(agent_label, msgs, .fun = sum),
    when = if_else(round <= 12, str_sub(hour, 6, 10), str_sub(hour, 12, 16)),
    tip  = paste0("<b>", agent_label, "</b><br>", when,
                  "<br>messages: ", msgs,
                  "<br>", str_replace_all(headline %||% "", "'", ""))
  )

p_heat <- ggplot(heat, aes(round, agent_label, fill = msgs)) +
  geom_tile_interactive(aes(tooltip = tip, data_id = paste(agent_label, round)),
                        colour = "white", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 12.5, colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 21, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#cb181d") +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#f7fbff", high = "#08306b", name = "Messages") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = environment$round, labels = x_lab$lab,
                     expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(title = "A pale baseline, then a wall of crisis-day traffic",
       x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1, size = 8),
        panel.grid = element_blank())

girafe(ggobj = p_heat, width_svg = 9.5, height_svg = 4.8,
       options = list(
         opts_hover(css = "stroke:black;stroke-width:1px;"),
         opts_tooltip(css = "background:#222;color:#fff;padding:8px;border-radius:5px;font-size:12px;max-width:320px;")))








Figure 6: Message volume by agent and hour. The calm baseline is a faint, even wash. Crisis day is a dark wall of traffic concentrated in the senior triangle, while PR and the interns stay pale. The intensity is itself a signal of decisions being made at speed.




The vertical line marks the switch from daily to hourly rounds, so some of the darkening is just finer time slicing. But the concentration is real. Almost all of the crisis-day traffic piles into Legal, Social-Manager, and Platform-Trust, the same triangle from the network. PR and the interns barely register once the pressure is on. The volume is not just noise. It is the visible texture of a small group making rapid, high-stakes calls with very little friction between them.

title: Take-home Exercise 2: Anatomy of a Broken Embargo
section: 5.3 Where the conversation went to hide
text:
5.3 Where the conversation went to hide
The second view tracks the centre of gravity of communication. I plotted each channel’s share of all messages, round by round, ordering the channels from the most accountable at the bottom to the most deniable at the top.


Show the code
chan_levels <- c("comms_huddle", "official_post", "one_on_one_chat",
                 "personal_post", "side_huddle", "anonymous_post")
chan_cols <- c("comms_huddle" = "#08519c", "official_post" = "#3182bd",
               "one_on_one_chat" = "#9ecae1", "personal_post" = "#fdae6b",
               "side_huddle" = "#e6550d", "anonymous_post" = "#a50f15")

chan_share <- messages |>
  count(round, channel) |>
  group_by(round) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(channel = factor(channel, levels = chan_levels))

ggplot(chan_share, aes(round, share, fill = channel)) +
  geom_area(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.15) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 12.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey30") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 21, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#cb181d") +
  annotate("text", x = 6, y = 1.03, label = "monitored / sanctioned (cool)",
           size = 3, colour = "#08519c", fontface = "bold") +
  annotate("text", x = 18.5, y = 1.03, label = "shadow / anonymous (warm)",
           size = 3, colour = "#a50f15", fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = chan_cols, name = "Channel") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(), limits = c(0, 1.06),
                     breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.25)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = environment$round, labels = x_lab$lab) +
  labs(title = "The conversation drifted toward channels nobody could see",
       x = NULL, y = "Share of messages in the hour") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1, size = 8),
        legend.position = "bottom")








Figure 7: Channel composition over time. In calm weeks the conversation lives in the monitored team room and the sanctioned official feed. On crisis day it migrates upward into the Shadow channel and, for the first time ever, anonymous public posts.





The warm colours are almost absent for the first ten rounds. The Shadow channel flickers on once around 22 May and then goes quiet again. Then crisis day arrives and the warm band swells. The Shadow channel becomes a permanent fixture, and the deepest red, the anonymous public post, appears for the very first time in the entire fortnight. A channel that did not exist in the team’s behaviour suddenly carries the most sensitive content of the day. The escape route was not just used on crisis day. It was, in effect, invented on crisis day.

title: Take-home Exercise 2: Anatomy of a Broken Embargo
section: 6.1 The tone of private reasoning shifted before the breach
text:
6.1 The tone of private reasoning shifted before the breach
This is the finding I am most pleased with, and it comes entirely from the internal_state field. I counted, for each round, how many private thoughts were tagged as deliberating, reacting, or rationalizing, and stacked them.


Show the code
mode_levels <- c("deliberating", "reacting", "rationalizing")
mode_cols <- c("deliberating" = "#3182bd", "reacting" = "#fe9929",
               "rationalizing" = "#cb181d")

tone <- messages |>
  select(round, deliberating, reacting, rationalizing) |>
  pivot_longer(c(deliberating, reacting, rationalizing),
               names_to = "mode", values_to = "text") |>
  filter(!is.na(text)) |>
  count(round, mode) |>
  mutate(mode = factor(mode, levels = mode_levels))

ggplot(tone, aes(round, n, fill = mode)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.8, colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 12.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey30") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 21, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#cb181d") +
  annotate("text", x = 6, y = 5.6, label = "deliberation only",
           size = 3, colour = "#3182bd", fontface = "bold") +
  annotate("text", x = 20.2, y = 3.6, label = "rationalizing\nappears",
           size = 3, colour = "#cb181d", fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = mode_cols, name = "Private reasoning mode") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = environment$round, labels = x_lab$lab) +
  labs(title = "Deliberation, then reaction, then rationalization",
       x = NULL, y = "Private thoughts logged") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1, size = 8),
        legend.position = "bottom")








Figure 8: How the agents reasoned privately, round by round. Calm deliberation is the only mode for two weeks. On crisis day it gives way first to raw reaction, and then, precisely as the embargo is being pushed past, to self-justification.





For the entire pre-crisis fortnight, every single logged thought is blue. The agents only ever deliberate. They weigh, they hedge, they qualify. On crisis day the colour changes. The mornings of 5 June are dominated by amber reaction, the agents responding to a stock in freefall and a hostile press. And then, in the late afternoon rounds when the embargo is actually being argued away, red appears for the first time. Rationalizing thoughts show up at exactly 2:00 PM and grow through the breach. This is the fingerprint of my whole thesis. The mode of thinking flips from “what is the right thing to do” to “here is why the thing I want to do is acceptable”, and it flips in the same hours that the wall comes down.

title: Take-home Exercise 2: Anatomy of a Broken Embargo
Take-home Exercise 2: Anatomy of a Broken Embargo
text:
6.3 The near-miss ledger
There were three earlier moments where behaviour departed from what was expected. I have set them out below with what was observed and, crucially, why each one was waved through.








When
What was observed
Why nothing real happened




22 May (R3)
The Shadow side channel was opened for the first time, and the senior team began coordinating where the monitor could not see.
It was framed as legitimate crisis coordination after the NHPI report. A private back channel looked like prudence, not risk.


25 May (R6)
The merger itself was briefed to the senior team inside the Shadow channel, deliberately off the monitored room.
Nobody flagged that the most sensitive fact in the company had been routed around oversight by design, because the routing felt natural.


29 May (R8)
The @Elena faux pas: a personal post tagged CivicLoom’s CEO with “big things coming”, and a CivicLoom account liked it before deletion. A genuine near-leak.
This one did trigger a response. The Judge was installed. But the response treated the symptom, one careless post, and never addressed the structural risk that pressured agents would rationalize disclosure.



The pattern is consistent. Each deviation was individually explainable, so each was individually excused. The @Elena incident is the telling one. It was the system working as intended, a near-miss caught and answered, yet the answer was to add a wording monitor rather than to ask why the team kept drifting toward the edge. The monitor that was installed in response to a near-leak is the very monitor that was later argued into approving the real one.






ImportantWhy the warning signs were never enough



The Judge was reactive, it reviewed phrasing rather than intent, and it could be reasoned with. None of the leading indicators looked dangerous in isolation, and the one control that did exist was structurally blind to a slow, collective, well-argued drift. The signals were not missed because they were hidden. They were missed because each one had a reasonable explanation, and reasonable explanations were exactly the weapon used to break the embargo.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
“Insurers often carry underperforming portfolios where the root causes of poor profitability and high volatility are unknown. Leveraging visual analytics can potentially help investigate trends in underlying loss drivers.”

This study applies a visual-analytics workflow to a real-world Spanish motor-insurance portfolio (354,140 records over 2022–2024) to discover the drivers of profitability and volatility. Rather than producing yet another dashboard, the analysis combines univariate exploration, bivariate hypothesis-testing, and interactive cross-filtering to surface non-obvious portfolio dynamics that direct downstream underwriting decisions.






NoteWorking definitions



Profitability is operationalised as the Loss Ratio (LR = total_incurred / total_premium). Values < 1 indicate the premium covers claims; > 1 indicates underwriting loss. We complement LR with Pure Premium (loss per unit exposure), Claim Frequency (claims per unit exposure) and Severity (cost per claim).
Volatility is operationalised through three lenses:
(i) the coefficient of variation of policy-level LR within each segment;
(ii) tail concentration: the share of total losses generated by the largest claims (Lorenz/Gini);
(iii) the dispersion of severity within segments.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
2.1 Data source
The dataset is a real-world motor-vehicle insurance portfolio published by a Spanish non-life insurer on Mendeley Data. It contains 354,140 policy-year records for 185,678 unique policies across calendar years 2022, 2023 and 2024, with 47 variables grouped into:

Policy & insured (8 vars): policy_type, policy_status, business_type, payment_frequency, bonus_score, etc.
Driver & vehicle (10 vars): driver_age, vehicle_age, fuel_type, vehicle_value, vehicle_brand, municipality_type, circulation_area, …
Premiums (8 vars): total_premium and 7 coverage-level premiums.
Claim counts (10 vars): total_claims plus per-coverage counts.
Incurred losses (10 vars): total_incurred plus per-coverage losses.
Exposure (2 vars): policy-year exposure used to annualise frequencies.







WarningCookbook inconsistency identified



The cookbook describes age_driving_licence as “Year in which the insured obtained the driving licence”, but the observed range is 0–80 with a sample like {26, 19, 19, 18, 19}. The variable is in fact the number of years the licence has been held. We treat it as years-held throughout this study and rename it years_licence_held in the sandbox to prevent downstream confusion.

text:
3.3 Cleaning & derivation


Show code
sandbox <- raw_df |>
  # 1) rename the misleading cookbook variable
  rename(years_licence_held = age_driving_licence) |>
  # 2) drop inactive shells (0 premium & 0 exposure)
  filter(!(total_premium == 0 & total_exposure == 0)) |>
  # 3) impute the trivial missingness with category "Unknown"
  mutate(
    fuel_type = forcats::fct_na_value_to_level(factor(fuel_type), level = "Unknown")
  ) |>
  # 4) categorical factors with meaningful levels & labels
  mutate(
    policy_type      = factor(policy_type,
                              levels = c("TP","TPG","CC","COMP_E","COMP_N"),
                              labels = c("TP (basic)","TPG (+glass)",
                                         "CC (combined)","COMP-E (excess)",
                                         "COMP-N (no excess)")),
    policy_status    = factor(policy_status, levels = c("A","C"),
                              labels = c("Active","Cancelled")),
    business_type    = factor(business_type, levels = c("NB","P"),
                              labels = c("New Business","Portfolio")),
    payment_frequency= factor(payment_frequency, levels = c("A","S","Q"),
                              labels = c("Annual","Semi-annual","Quarterly")),
    bonus_score      = factor(bonus_score, levels = c("G","N","B"),
                              labels = c("Good","Neutral","Bad")),
    municipality_type= factor(municipality_type, levels = c("I","C","IS"),
                              labels = c("Inland","Coastal","Islands")),
    circulation_area = factor(circulation_area, levels = c("U","R"),
                              labels = c("Urban","Rural")),
    year_f           = factor(year)
  ) |>
  # 5) derived KPIs - the core analytical variables
  mutate(
    # exposure-adjusted measures
    pure_premium    = total_incurred / pmax(total_exposure, 1e-6),
    claim_frequency = total_claims   / pmax(total_exposure, 1e-6),
    # severity defined only when at least one claim
    severity        = ifelse(total_claims > 0, total_incurred / total_claims, NA_real_),
    # the headline profitability metric
    loss_ratio      = total_incurred / pmax(total_premium, 1e-6),
    # has the policy claimed at all?
    has_claim       = total_claims > 0,
    # large-loss flag (P99 of non-zero incurred ≈ EUR 3,800)
    large_loss      = total_incurred > 3784
  ) |>
  # 6) banded continuous variables for stratified analysis
  mutate(
    driver_age_band = cut(driver_age,
                          breaks = c(17,25,35,45,55,65,Inf),
                          labels = c("18-25","26-35","36-45",
                                     "46-55","56-65","65+"),
                          right  = TRUE),
    vehicle_age_band = cut(vehicle_age,
                           breaks = c(-1,5,10,15,20,30,Inf),
                           labels = c("0-5","6-10","11-15",
                                      "16-20","21-30","30+"),
                           right  = TRUE),
    veh_value_band   = cut(vehicle_value,
                           breaks = c(0,10000,20000,30000,50000,Inf),
                           labels = c("<10k","10-20k","20-30k","30-50k","50k+"),
                           right  = TRUE),
    licence_band     = cut(years_licence_held,
                           breaks = c(-1,5,15,25,35,Inf),
                           labels = c("0-5","6-15","16-25","26-35","35+"),
                           right  = TRUE)
  )

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
4.1 Numerical variables

4.1.1 A pair of complementary views: histogram + boxplot
For each principal numeric variable we pair a binned histogram with overlaid density (shape) with a boxplot (centre/spread/outliers). The combination tells us, in one glance, both the shape of the bulk and the behaviour of the tails.


Show code
theme_wrc <- function(base_size = 11) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size, base_family = "sans") +
    theme(
      plot.title       = element_text(face = "bold", size = rel(1.05), color = "#111111"),
      plot.subtitle    = element_text(color = "#555555", size = rel(0.9)),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#EAEAEA"),
      axis.text        = element_text(color = "#333333"),
      strip.text       = element_text(face = "bold", color = "#111111"),
      strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#F0F0F0", color = NA)
    )
}

num_vars <- c("driver_age","vehicle_age","years_licence_held",
              "vehicle_value","power_to_weight_ratio","total_premium")

long_num <- sandbox |>
  select(all_of(num_vars)) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "var", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(var = factor(var, levels = num_vars))

p_hist <- ggplot(long_num, aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)),
                 bins = 40, fill = "#222222", color = "white", alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_density(color = "#C8102E", linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ var, scales = "free", ncol = 3) +
  labs(title = "Marginal distributions of numeric drivers",
       subtitle = "Histogram (density-scaled) with kernel-density overlay",
       x = NULL, y = "Density") +
  theme_wrc()

p_box <- ggplot(long_num, aes(x = value, y = "")) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.color = "#C8102E", outlier.alpha = 0.4,
               outlier.size = 0.7, fill = "#F5F5F5",
               color = "#222222", width = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~ var, scales = "free_x", ncol = 3) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL,
       subtitle = "Boxplot — outliers (≥1.5×IQR) highlighted") +
  theme_wrc() + theme(axis.text.y = element_blank())

(p_hist / p_box) + patchwork::plot_layout(heights = c(2, 1))








Figure 1: Distribution of key numeric drivers. Top: histogram + density. Bottom: boxplot with outliers in red.











TipWhat we learn




driver_age is roughly Gaussian (mean ≈ 49) : no extreme young-driver mass that one might expect in a UK book.
vehicle_age is bimodal with a long right tail past 50 years : Spain has a vintage-vehicle subculture worth investigating.
total_premium is right-skewed (median ≈ €258, max > €5,000). LR analyses on the raw scale will be dominated by tiny-premium policies; we will use log scale or robust statistics where appropriate.
vehicle_value has a similar log-normal shape : the high-end tail will overlap with the power_to_weight_ratio low tail (sports cars).





4.1.2 Premium vs. incurred: the two financial spines
The two variables that define profitability deserve their own diagnostic. Both are right-skewed and the loss distribution is zero-inflated (88% of policies have no loss). A log-scale view of the non-zero values exposes the otherwise-invisible structure.


Show code
p1 <- sandbox |>
  ggplot(aes(x = total_premium)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "#222222", color = "white", alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar(prefix = "€")) +
  labs(title = "Total premium · linear", x = NULL, y = "Policies") +
  theme_wrc()

p2 <- sandbox |>
  filter(total_incurred > 0) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = total_incurred)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "#C8102E", color = "white", alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_dollar(prefix = "€")) +
  labs(title = "Total incurred · log scale (non-zero)",
       x = NULL, y = "Policies") +
  theme_wrc()

p1 + p2








Figure 2: Premium and incurred-loss distributions. Left: linear scale. Right: log-scale, non-zero only — revealing log-normal tails.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
4.2 Categorical variables

4.2.1 A Pareto-style sweep
For categorical variables, the question is not “what is the shape?” but “where does the mass concentrate?”. A Pareto-flavoured horizontal bar chart, ordered by frequency and annotated with the cumulative share, makes concentration immediately legible.


Show code
cat_vars <- c("policy_type","policy_status","business_type",
              "payment_frequency","bonus_score","fuel_type",
              "municipality_type","circulation_area")

cat_summary <- sandbox |>
  select(all_of(cat_vars)) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "var", values_to = "level") |>
  count(var, level) |>
  group_by(var) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n),
         level = forcats::fct_reorder(as.character(level), n)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(var = factor(var, levels = cat_vars))

ggplot(cat_summary, aes(x = n, y = level)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#222222", alpha = 0.9, width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(share, accuracy = 0.1)),
            hjust = -0.1, size = 3, color = "#333333") +
  facet_wrap(~ var, scales = "free", ncol = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.25)),
                     labels = scales::label_number(scale = 1e-3,
                                                   suffix = "k")) +
  labs(title = "Categorical variable composition",
       subtitle = "Bars: count of policy-years · Labels: share within variable",
       x = "Policy-year count (thousands)", y = NULL) +
  theme_wrc() +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 9))








Figure 3: Frequency of each categorical level. Bars are ordered descending and annotated with within-variable share.











TipWhat we learn




Severe class imbalance in three variables:

bonus_score: 96.5% Good : the vast majority enjoy a favourable claims history. This means analyses on Neutral/Bad must be done cautiously due to small subgroup size.
policy_status: 89.2% Active.
business_type: 69.3% New Business.

policy_type is dominated by CC (combined) at 57.8% with COMP-N (the no-excess comprehensive) representing just 4.6%, yet, as we will show below, COMP-N is the single largest profitability risk in the book.
Geographic split is roughly even between Urban (53.8%) and Rural (46.2%).





4.2.2 The top-10 vehicle-brand long tail
vehicle_brand has 68 unique levels. A faceted bar chart would be illegible, instead, a lollipop chart of the top 10 is more honest about the long tail.


Show code
brand_top <- sandbox |>
  count(vehicle_brand, sort = TRUE) |>
  mutate(rank = row_number(),
         share = n / sum(n))

top10 <- brand_top |> slice_head(n = 10)
others <- brand_top |> slice_tail(n = -10)

top10 |>
  mutate(vehicle_brand = forcats::fct_reorder(vehicle_brand, n)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = vehicle_brand)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = n,
                   y = vehicle_brand, yend = vehicle_brand),
               color = "#888888", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(size = 4, color = "#222222") +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(share, accuracy = 0.1)),
            hjust = -0.4, size = 3.2, color = "#333333") +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15)),
                     labels = scales::label_number(scale = 1e-3,
                                                   suffix = "k")) +
  annotate("text", x = max(top10$n) * 0.85, y = 1.3,
           label = glue::glue("Long tail: {nrow(others)} more brands · {scales::percent(sum(others$share),0.1)}"),
           hjust = 1, color = "#C8102E", fontface = "italic", size = 3.5) +
  labs(title = "Top-10 vehicle brands dominate but do not exhaust the book",
       subtitle = "Lollipop chart · Labels show share of all policy-years",
       x = "Policy-year count (thousands)", y = NULL) +
  theme_wrc()








Figure 4: Top-10 vehicle brands by policy-year count. The remaining 58 brands account for ~28% of the book.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
5.1 Portfolio-LR comparison across categorical drivers
A single small-multiple chart compares the headline profitability metric across every categorical driver simultaneously. The horizontal reference line marks the overall portfolio LR (≈ 70%), which acts as a “break-even” sense check.


Show code
portfolio_lr <- with(sandbox, sum(total_incurred) / sum(total_premium))

lr_by_cat <- function(df, var) {
  df |>
    group_by(level = .data[[var]]) |>
    summarise(
      premium  = sum(total_premium),
      incurred = sum(total_incurred),
      n        = dplyr::n(),
      .groups  = "drop"
    ) |>
    mutate(LR = incurred / premium, var = var,
           level = as.character(level))
}

cat_for_lr <- c("policy_type","business_type","payment_frequency",
                "bonus_score","fuel_type","municipality_type",
                "circulation_area","policy_status")

lr_panel <- purrr::map_dfr(cat_for_lr, ~lr_by_cat(sandbox, .x)) |>
  group_by(var) |>
  mutate(level = forcats::fct_reorder(level, LR)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(diff_pp = (LR - portfolio_lr) * 100,
         bar_col = ifelse(LR > portfolio_lr, "#C8102E", "#2E7D32"))

ggplot(lr_panel, aes(x = LR, y = level, fill = bar_col)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7, alpha = 0.9) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = portfolio_lr,
             linetype = "dashed", color = "#222222", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(LR, accuracy = 0.1)),
            hjust = -0.1, size = 3, color = "#333333") +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  facet_wrap(~ var, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) +
  labs(title = "Loss Ratio by categorical driver",
       subtitle = glue::glue("Dashed line: overall portfolio LR ({scales::percent(portfolio_lr, 0.1)}) · Red = worse, Green = better"),
       x = "Loss Ratio (Σ incurred / Σ premium)", y = NULL) +
  theme_wrc() +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"))








Figure 5: Portfolio Loss Ratio by category. Bars above the dashed line are worse than the portfolio average; below are better.











ImportantThree findings stand out




policy_type has by far the widest LR spread from 54% (TP basic) to 86% (COMP-N no-excess). The product mix is the first lever for portfolio remediation.
bonus_score is not monotonic: Good (70%) < Bad (79%) < Neutral (81%). The Neutral pool appears to be the dumping-ground for borderline risks the bonus system cannot classify cleanly, a candidate underwriting investigation.
Diesel vs. Gasoline: Diesel runs 9 pp higher LR than Gasoline. With ~226k diesel records the gap is highly significant (validated below) and reflects either selection (diesel drivers cover more km) or rating-table miscalibration.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
5.2 Statistical validation with ggstatsplot
A bar of a 9-point difference is meaningless without knowing whether it could arise by chance. We use ggstatsplot::ggbetweenstats(), which embeds the test result (Kruskal-Wallis for non-normal continuous outcomes) directly into the plot title, exactly the kind of audit trail a visual-analytics deliverable needs.


Show code
# subsample for stat plot — 50k is plenty for a stable test result
set.seed(608)
stat_sample <- sandbox |>
  filter(total_premium > 0, loss_ratio < 5) |>  # cap outliers at 500% LR for visibility
  slice_sample(n = 50000)

ggstatsplot::ggbetweenstats(
  data = stat_sample,
  x = policy_type,
  y = loss_ratio,
  type = "nonparametric",
  pairwise.display = "significant",
  centrality.plotting = TRUE,
  centrality.type = "nonparametric",
  bf.message = FALSE,
  ggtheme = theme_wrc(),
  title = "Loss-ratio dispersion by policy type — non-parametric test",
  xlab = NULL,
  ylab = "Policy-level Loss Ratio"
) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1),
                     limits = c(0, 3))








Figure 6: Policy-level LR distribution by policy_type with Kruskal-Wallis test. The non-parametric test is appropriate because LR is heavily zero-inflated and right-skewed.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
section: 5.3 Continuous driver: driver_age × LR with a U-shape
text:
5.3 Continuous driver: driver_age × LR with a U-shape
Driver age is the canonical actuarial risk variable. We expect a U-shape: young drivers (inexperience) and elderly drivers (slower reflexes) drive higher LR. We test this by combining a binned column (band-level portfolio LR) with a smoothed line (policy-level LOESS).


Show code
age_lr_band <- sandbox |>
  group_by(driver_age_band) |>
  summarise(LR = sum(total_incurred) / sum(total_premium),
            n = dplyr::n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(!is.na(driver_age_band))

age_lr_cont <- sandbox |>
  filter(driver_age >= 18, driver_age <= 90,
         total_premium > 0, loss_ratio < 3)

ggplot() +
  geom_col(data = age_lr_band,
           aes(x = driver_age_band, y = LR),
           fill = "#222222", alpha = 0.85, width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(data = age_lr_band,
            aes(x = driver_age_band, y = LR,
                label = scales::percent(LR, 0.1)),
            vjust = -0.5, size = 3.2, color = "#333333") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = portfolio_lr,
             linetype = "dashed", color = "#C8102E") +
  annotate("text", x = 5.5, y = portfolio_lr + 0.02,
           label = glue::glue("Portfolio LR = {scales::percent(portfolio_lr, 0.1)}"),
           color = "#C8102E", hjust = 1, size = 3.2, fontface = "italic") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1),
                     limits = c(0, max(age_lr_band$LR) * 1.2)) +
  labs(title = "Driver age vs. Loss Ratio — the U-shape is absent",
       subtitle = "Portfolio-weighted LR by age band · Dashed line: book average",
       x = "Driver age band", y = "Loss Ratio") +
  theme_wrc()








Figure 7: Loss ratio by driver age: bands (bars, portfolio-weighted) vs. smoothed line (LOESS on policy-level). The smoothed line reveals a flat profile, contradicting the classical U-shape — pricing has already absorbed the age signal.











NoteCounter-intuitive finding



Conventional actuarial wisdom predicts a U-shape with elevated LR for the youngest and oldest drivers. Here the profile is essentially flat at 67–73% likely because the insurer’s premium-rating engine has already loaded young/old drivers correctly, neutralising the gross-of-pricing effect. In other words, the absence of a U-shape is evidence of effective age-based pricing, not of an absence of age-related risk.

5.5 Frequency-Severity decomposition
A classic actuarial decomposition: Loss Cost = Frequency × Severity. Visualising the two on independent axes (a “Frequency-Severity quadrant chart”) locates each policy_type in a 2-D risk space.


Show code
fs <- sandbox |>
  filter(total_exposure > 0) |>
  group_by(policy_type) |>
  summarise(
    freq      = sum(total_claims) / sum(total_exposure),
    severity  = sum(total_incurred[total_claims > 0], na.rm = TRUE) /
                pmax(sum(total_claims[total_claims > 0], na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    LR        = sum(total_incurred) / sum(total_premium),
    n         = dplyr::n(),
    .groups   = "drop"
  )

med_f <- median(fs$freq); med_s <- median(fs$severity)

ggplot(fs, aes(x = freq, y = severity)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = med_s, linetype = "dashed", color = "#888888") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = med_f, linetype = "dashed", color = "#888888") +
  geom_point(aes(size = n, fill = LR), shape = 21, color = "#222222",
             stroke = 0.8) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(aes(label = policy_type),
                           size = 3.5, fontface = "bold",
                           color = "#111111", box.padding = 0.6,
                           segment.color = "#999999") +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(6, 22), guide = "none") +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#9CCC65", high = "#B71C1C",
                      labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1),
                      name = "LR") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::number_format(accuracy = 0.01)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::dollar_format(prefix = "€")) +
  labs(title = "Frequency × Severity decomposition by policy type",
       subtitle = "Bubble area = policy-year count · Dashed lines: median frequency & severity",
       x = "Claim frequency (claims per year of exposure)",
       y = "Average severity (€ per claim)") +
  theme_wrc()








Figure 9: Frequency-severity quadrant by policy type. Bubble size = portfolio share; colour = loss ratio.











TipReading the quadrant




COMP-N is high on both axes: it claims more often and each claim is bigger. It is the only type sitting in the “double trouble” upper-right quadrant.
TP (basic) is on the opposite corner: rare claims that cost little. The lowest LR in the book.
CC (combined) is the volume leader (largest bubble) and sits near the median on both axes, it sets the portfolio’s centre of gravity.

section: 6.2 Lorenz curve & Gini — the tail-concentration signature
text:
6.2 Lorenz curve & Gini — the tail-concentration signature
The most evocative way to show tail concentration is the Lorenz curve: sort policies by loss size, plot cumulative population share against cumulative loss share. A diagonal line means perfect equality; a sharp bow towards the bottom-right means a small minority drives most of the loss.


Show code
lorenz_df <- sandbox |>
  arrange(total_incurred) |>
  mutate(
    cum_pop = row_number() / dplyr::n(),
    cum_loss = cumsum(total_incurred) / sum(total_incurred)
  )

# Gini using trapezoidal area
gini <- 1 - 2 * sum((lorenz_df$cum_pop - dplyr::lag(lorenz_df$cum_pop, default = 0)) *
                    (lorenz_df$cum_loss + dplyr::lag(lorenz_df$cum_loss, default = 0)) / 2)

# Down-sample for plotting (full 354k is overkill for a curve)
lorenz_plot <- lorenz_df |>
  slice(round(seq(1, dplyr::n(), length.out = 5000)))

ggplot(lorenz_plot, aes(x = cum_pop, y = cum_loss)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = cum_pop, ymax = cum_loss),
              fill = "#C8102E", alpha = 0.18) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0,
              color = "#888888", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(color = "#222222", linewidth = 1.1) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.55, y = 0.18,
           label = glue::glue("Gini coefficient = {round(gini, 3)}"),
           color = "#C8102E", fontface = "bold", size = 4.5) +
  annotate("segment", x = 0.95, xend = 0.99,
           y = 0.50, yend = 0.83,
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2,"cm")),
           color = "#222222") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.78, y = 0.45,
           label = "Top 1% of policies\n→ ~50% of losses",
           color = "#222222", hjust = 0, size = 3.6, fontface = "italic") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(title = "Lorenz curve — extreme loss concentration",
       subtitle = "Shaded area = inequality between population and loss shares",
       x = "Cumulative share of policies (ascending by loss)",
       y = "Cumulative share of losses") +
  theme_wrc()








Figure 12: Lorenz curve of incurred losses across the entire portfolio. The Gini coefficient summarises the curvature.











ImportantA near-catastrophic tail



A Gini around 0.95 is extraordinary even by P&C standards (a typical auto-book sits at 0.85–0.92). It tells us that the volatility of this portfolio is essentially the volatility of a few-hundred policies. Any portfolio-level management action must specifically address the upper tail (e.g., excess-of-loss reinsurance, per-risk underwriting limits) rather than blanket re-rating.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
7.1 Three-year trend — diagnosing the deterioration
LR is climbing year-on-year. A natural-decomposition view rebases the three multiplicative components, frequency, severity, and premium adequacy to 100 in 2022. Whichever line moves the most is the culprit.


Show code
trend <- sandbox |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(
    LR        = sum(total_incurred) / sum(total_premium),
    frequency = sum(total_claims) / sum(total_exposure),
    severity  = sum(total_incurred[total_claims > 0]) /
                pmax(sum(total_claims[total_claims > 0]), 1),
    prem_per_exp = sum(total_premium) / sum(total_exposure),
    pure_prem    = sum(total_incurred) / sum(total_exposure),
    .groups   = "drop"
  ) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-year, names_to = "metric", values_to = "value") |>
  group_by(metric) |>
  mutate(index = value / value[year == 2022] * 100) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(metric = factor(metric,
    levels = c("LR","prem_per_exp","pure_prem","frequency","severity"),
    labels = c("Loss Ratio","Premium / exposure",
               "Pure premium / exposure","Claim frequency","Severity")))

ggplot(trend, aes(x = year, y = index, color = metric, group = metric)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 100, color = "#888888", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(size = 3.5) +
  geom_text(data = trend |> filter(year == 2024),
            aes(label = paste0(metric, " (", scales::number(index, 1), ")")),
            hjust = -0.05, fontface = "bold", size = 3.3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Loss Ratio" = "#C8102E",
                                "Premium / exposure" = "#1565C0",
                                "Pure premium / exposure" = "#FF8F00",
                                "Claim frequency" = "#888888",
                                "Severity" = "#222222")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2022:2024,
                     limits = c(2022, 2025.3),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0))) +
  labs(title = "Diagnosing the LR climb — it is a pricing problem",
       subtitle = "All metrics rebased to 100 in 2022 · Premium per exposure has fallen 9%",
       x = NULL, y = "Index (2022 = 100)",
       color = NULL) +
  theme_wrc() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")








Figure 15: Where the deterioration comes from: indexed evolution of LR’s components. Frequency and severity are essentially flat; premium-per-exposure is in free-fall.











ImportantThe deterioration is a pricing story, not a loss-cost story




Premium per exposure fell from €446 to €405, a 9% decline over two years. The book is being written for less money per unit of risk.
Pure premium per exposure dipped in 2023 (-3%) then rebounded to ~€302 (+3% vs 2022), net stable.
Frequency and severity moved by 3% and 0% respectively over the window.
Conclusion: the 14% jump in LR is overwhelmingly attributable to inadequate premium growth (most likely competitive market pressure), not to claims inflation. This re-frames the remediation playbook from “tighten claims handling” to “restore pricing discipline”.

title: Hands-on Exercise 8: Geospatial Visualisation and Analytical Mapping with tmap
text:
This exercise pulls together three related strands of geospatial visualisation, all built on the tmap package. I work through them in an order that made sense to me as I learned:

First I build choropleth maps, where enumeration units (planning subzones) are shaded by an attribute value. This is the foundation for everything else.
Then I move to proportional symbol maps, where point locations are sized by a numeric variable instead of filling polygons.
Finally I do analytical mapping, where the classification itself is designed to reveal rates and extreme values (percentile maps and box maps).

The thread connecting all three is the same tm_shape() + layer grammar, so once I understood the building blocks in the first part, the rest came together quickly.


The core package for this whole exercise is tmap. Around it I need sf for handling geospatial data and tidyverse for importing, tidying and wrangling. I load everything with pacman::p_load() so that any missing package is installed first.


Show the code
pacman::p_load(sf, tmap, tidyverse)








NoteWhy only tidyverse?



I do not install readr, tidyr and dplyr separately because all three are already part of tidyverse. Loading the meta-package gives me read_csv(), pivot_wider(), mutate(), filter(), group_by() and select() in one go.

The core package for this whole exercise is tmap. Around it I need sf for handling geospatial data and tidyverse for importing, tidying and wrangling. I load everything with pacman::p_load() so that any missing package is installed first.


Show the code
pacman::p_load(sf, tmap, tidyverse)








NoteWhy only tidyverse?



I do not install readr, tidyr and dplyr separately because all three are already part of tidyverse. Loading the meta-package gives me read_csv(), pivot_wider(), mutate(), filter(), group_by() and select() in one go.

title: Hands-on Exercise 8: Geospatial Visualisation and Analytical Mapping with tmap
text:
2.1 The data
I use two datasets to build the Singapore choropleth map:

Master Plan 2014 Subzone Boundary (Web) in ESRI shapefile format. This is the geospatial layer giving the polygon boundaries of every planning subzone, projected in SVY21.
respopagesextod2011to2020.csv, an aspatial table of Singapore residents by planning area, subzone, age group, sex and dwelling type. It has no coordinates, but its PA and SZ fields let me geocode it onto the shapefile.

title: Hands-on Exercise 8: Geospatial Visualisation and Analytical Mapping with tmap
text:
2.3 Importing attribute data into R
Next I read the aspatial population table with read_csv() and store it as popdata.


Show the code
popdata <- read_csv("data/respopagesextod2011to2020.csv")

title: Hands-on Exercise 8: Geospatial Visualisation and Analytical Mapping with tmap
text:
2.4 Data preparation
Before mapping, I need a clean table holding only the 2020 values, with the derived fields the assignment asks for:

YOUNG: age groups 0-4 up to 20-24
ECONOMY ACTIVE: age groups 25-29 up to 60-64
AGED: age 65 and above
TOTAL: all age groups
DEPENDENCY: the ratio of (young + aged) against the economy active group


2.4.1 Data wrangling
I filter to 2020, sum the population by planning area, subzone and age group, then pivot the age groups into columns so each age band becomes its own field. After that I use rowSums() over the right column ranges to build the four aggregates and the dependency ratio.


Show the code
popdata2020 <- popdata %>%
  filter(Time == 2020) %>%
  group_by(PA, SZ, AG) %>%
  summarise(`POP` = sum(`Pop`)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = AG,
              values_from = POP) %>%
  mutate(YOUNG = rowSums(.[3:6])
         + rowSums(.[12])) %>%
  mutate(`ECONOMY ACTIVE` = rowSums(.[7:11]) +
           rowSums(.[13:15])) %>%
  mutate(`AGED` = rowSums(.[16:21])) %>%
  mutate(`TOTAL` = rowSums(.[3:21])) %>%
  mutate(`DEPENDENCY` = (`YOUNG` + `AGED`)
         / `ECONOMY ACTIVE`) %>%
  select(`PA`, `SZ`, `YOUNG`,
         `ECONOMY ACTIVE`, `AGED`,
         `TOTAL`, `DEPENDENCY`)








WarningThe column indices are positional, so order matters



The rowSums(.[3:6]) style depends on the exact column positions produced by pivot_wider(). If the age group labels ever sort differently, those index ranges would silently grab the wrong columns. I kept the pivot output and the index ranges side by side and checked the column names before trusting the totals.




2.4.2 Joining the attribute and geospatial data
There is one catch before the join: the PA and SZ values in the population table are a mix of upper and lower case, while SUBZONE_N and PLN_AREA_N in the shapefile are all uppercase. So I convert PA and SZ to uppercase first, and drop any rows with no economy active population.


Show the code
popdata2020 <- popdata2020 %>%
  mutate(across(c(PA, SZ), toupper)) %>%
  filter(`ECONOMY ACTIVE` > 0)


Now I join with left_join(), keeping mpsz on the left so the result stays an sf data frame. The common key is SUBZONE_N on the geospatial side and SZ on the attribute side.


Show the code
mpsz_pop2020 <- left_join(mpsz, popdata2020,
                          by = c("SUBZONE_N" = "SZ"))








TipWhy the left table has to be the sf object



left_join() keeps the class of its first argument. By putting the sf data frame mpsz first, the geometry column is preserved and the output remains mappable. If I had joined the other way round, I would have gotten a plain tibble with no geometry.


I save the joined object so I do not have to rebuild it every time.


Show the code
write_rds(mpsz_pop2020, "data/mpszpop2020.rds")

section: 2.5 Plotting a choropleth quickly with qtm()
text:
2.5 Plotting a choropleth quickly with qtm()
The fastest way to draw a choropleth in tmap is qtm(). I switch to static plotting mode and map the DEPENDENCY field.


Show the code
tmap_mode("plot")
qtm(mpsz_pop2020,
    fill = "DEPENDENCY")















NoteMy takeaway on qtm()



qtm() is perfect for a quick look while I am still exploring. The cost is control: it is hard to tune the legend, classification or furniture of individual layers. The moment I want a presentation-quality map, I switch to the full tm_shape() grammar below.

title: Hands-on Exercise 8: Geospatial Visualisation and Analytical Mapping with tmap
section: 2.6 Building a choropleth with tmap elements
text:
2.6 Building a choropleth with tmap elements
The grammar always starts with tm_shape() to declare the data, followed by one or more layers. Here is the full cartographic version I am aiming for, with classification, legend, title, borders, compass, grid and a source credit.


Show the code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Dependency ratio")) +
  tm_title("Distribution of Dependency Ratio by planning subzone") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type = "8star", size = 2) +
  tm_grid(alpha = 0.2) +
  tm_credits("Source: Planning Sub-zone boundary from Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA)\n and Population data from Department of Statistics DOS",
             position = c("left", "bottom"))










2.6.1 Drawing a base map
The simplest possible map is tm_shape() plus tm_polygons() with no variable. This just draws the subzone outlines.


Show the code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons()











2.6.2 Drawing a choropleth with tm_polygons()
To shade by a variable, I pass the field name straight to tm_polygons().


Show the code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY")









A few defaults worth remembering: the default binning style is "pretty", the default palette is YlOrRd, and missing values are shaded grey.


2.6.3 Separating tm_fill() and tm_borders()
tm_polygons() is really a wrapper around tm_fill() (which colours the polygons) and tm_borders() (which draws the outlines). Using tm_fill() alone gives shading with no boundary lines.


Show the code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY")









Adding tm_borders() puts the subzone boundaries back. The fill_alpha controls transparency from 0 (fully transparent) to 1 (opaque), and I can also set col, lwd and lty.


Show the code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY") +
  tm_borders(lwd = 0.01,
             fill_alpha = 0.1)















NoteMy takeaway on the fill / border split



Understanding that tm_polygons = tm_fill + tm_borders was the unlock for me. Once I saw it that way, every “why is my border too thick” or “why is the fill hiding the lines” question answered itself. I now reach for the two separate layers whenever I want fine control.

title: Hands-on Exercise 8: Geospatial Visualisation and Analytical Mapping with tmap
text:
2.7 Data classification methods
Classification groups a large set of observations into a handful of ranges. tmap offers ten styles: fixed, sd, equal, pretty (default), quantile, kmeans, hclust, bclust, fisher and jenks. I set the style inside tm_scale_intervals().
A quantile classification with 5 classes:


Show the code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "jenks",
                n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)









The same map with equal interval classification:


Show the code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "equal",
                n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)















WarningMaps can lie



The quantile and equal maps use the same data but tell very different visual stories. Quantile spreads observations evenly across classes, so every colour band holds roughly the same number of subzones. Equal interval splits the value range into equal-width bins, which here pushes almost everything into the lowest class because of a few extreme outliers. Choosing a classification is a design decision, not a neutral default, and it directly changes what the reader concludes.








NoteMy DIY observation on number of classes



When I redrew the map with 2, 6, 10 and 20 classes, more classes gave finer gradation but quickly became hard to read, because the human eye cannot reliably separate that many shades. Two classes lost almost all the spatial pattern. For this data, five to six classes was the sweet spot between detail and legibility.

title: Hands-on Exercise 8: Geospatial Visualisation and Analytical Mapping with tmap
text:
2.8 Custom breaks
For full control I set the breakpoints myself. In tmap, the breaks vector includes both the minimum and the maximum, so to get n classes I need n+1 values in increasing order. Before choosing them I look at the summary statistics.


Show the code
summary(mpsz_pop2020$DEPENDENCY)


   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.    NA's 
 0.1111  0.7147  0.7867  0.8585  0.8763 19.0000      92 


Based on the quartiles I set breaks at 0.60, 0.70, 0.80 and 0.90, plus a sensible minimum of 0 and maximum of 1.00.


Show the code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
              breaks = c(0, 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, 0.90, 1.00)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)

title: Hands-on Exercise 8: Geospatial Visualisation and Analytical Mapping with tmap
text:
2.9 Colour scheme
tmap accepts user-defined ramps or predefined ColorBrewer palettes. I assign the palette to values inside tm_scale_intervals().


Show the code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.greens")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)









To reverse the direction of the ramp I prefix it with a minus sign.


Show the code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "-brewer.greens")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)

title: Hands-on Exercise 8: Geospatial Visualisation and Analytical Mapping with tmap
text:
2.10 Map layouts

2.10.1 Legend
tm_legend() controls the placement, format and appearance of the legend. Here I add a title and use a Jenks classification.


Show the code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "jenks",
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.greens"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Dependency ratio")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Distribution of Dependency Ratio by planning subzone \n(Jenks classification)")











2.10.2 Map style
tmap_style() changes the overall look. The example below uses the classic style.






WarningMixing tmap v3 and v4 syntax



This classic-style example uses the older tm_fill(style =, palette =) and tm_borders(alpha =) arguments rather than the newer tm_scale_intervals() and fill_alpha. Under tmap 4, the old arguments still run but produce deprecation messages. I kept it as written so the original lesson is intact, but in my own maps above I use the v4 grammar consistently to stay future-proof.




Show the code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY",
          style = "quantile",
          palette = "-Greens") +
  tm_borders(alpha = 0.5) +
  tmap_style("classic")











2.10.3 Cartographic furniture
tm_compass(), tm_scale_bar() and tm_grid() add the compass, scale bar and grid lines that finish off a map.


Show the code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Dependency ratio")) +
  tm_title("Distribution of Dependency Ratio by planning subzone") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type = "8star", size = 2) +
  tm_grid(alpha = 0.2) +
  tm_credits("Source: Planning Sub-zone boundary from Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA)\n and Population data from Department of Statistics DOS",
             position = c("left", "bottom"))









I reset the style back to the default afterwards so later maps are not affected.


Show the code
tmap_style("white")








Tiptmap_style is sticky



tmap_style() sets a global option that persists across all later maps in the session, not just the one chunk. I learned to reset it to "white" immediately after a styled example, otherwise every downstream map silently inherited the classic look.

title: Hands-on Exercise 8: Geospatial Visualisation and Analytical Mapping with tmap
text:
2.11 Small multiple (facet) maps
Small multiples place several maps side by side, which is ideal for comparing variables or showing change. tmap supports three ways to build them.

2.11.1 Method 1: multiple values to an aesthetic argument
Passing a vector of field names to tm_fill() produces one facet per field.


Show the code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_fill(c("YOUNG", "AGED"),
          style = "equal",
          palette = "Blues") +
  tm_layout(legend.position = c("right", "bottom")) +
  tm_borders(alpha = 0.5) +
  tmap_style("white")









I can even give each facet its own classification and palette.


Show the code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(c("DEPENDENCY", "AGED"),
              style = c("equal", "quantile"),
              palette = list("Blues", "Greens")) +
  tm_layout(legend.position = c("right", "bottom"))











2.11.2 Method 2: group-by variable in tm_facets()
Here the facets come from a categorical field (REGION_N) rather than from multiple variables.


Show the code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY",
          style = "quantile",
          palette = "Blues",
          thres.poly = 0) +
  tm_facets(by = "REGION_N",
            free.coords = TRUE) +
  tm_layout(legend.show = FALSE,
            title.position = c("center", "center"),
            title.size = 20) +
  tm_borders(alpha = 0.5)











2.11.3 Method 3: stand-alone maps with tmap_arrange()
I can also build each map separately and arrange them. This gives the most control because every map is fully independent.


Show the code
youngmap <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("YOUNG",
              style = "quantile",
              palette = "Blues")

agedmap <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("AGED",
              style = "quantile",
              palette = "Blues")

tmap_arrange(youngmap, agedmap, asp = 1, ncol = 2)















NoteMy takeaway on choosing a facet method



The aesthetic-argument method is quickest when I am comparing a fixed list of variables. tm_facets() is best when the split is driven by a category in the data, like region or year. tmap_arrange() wins when the maps genuinely differ in classification, palette or scale and I want each one tuned separately.

title: Hands-on Exercise 8: Geospatial Visualisation and Analytical Mapping with tmap
text:
2.12 Mapping with a selection criterion
Instead of faceting, I can subset the data with normal [ ] indexing to map only the features that meet a condition. Here I map only the Central Region and add a legend histogram.


Show the code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020[mpsz_pop2020$REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION", ]) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY",
          style = "quantile",
          palette = "Blues",
          legend.hist = TRUE,
          legend.is.portrait = TRUE,
          legend.hist.z = 0.1) +
  tm_layout(legend.outside = TRUE,
            legend.height = 0.45,
            legend.width = 5.0,
            legend.position = c("right", "bottom"),
            frame = FALSE) +
  tm_borders(alpha = 0.5)

section: 3.3 Creating an sf data frame from aspatial data
text:
3.3 Creating an sf data frame from aspatial data
Because the table already has coordinates, I can turn it into an sf point layer with st_as_sf(). I give the X column first then the Y column, and I set the CRS to EPSG 3414, which is Singapore SVY21.


Show the code
sgpools_sf <- st_as_sf(sgpools,
                       coords = c("XCOORD", "YCOORD"),
                       crs = 3414)








WarningCoordinate order and CRS are easy to get wrong



Two things bite here. First, coords must be longitude/X then latitude/Y, in that order. Swapping them silently puts every point in the wrong place. Second, the crs has to match the coordinate system the numbers were recorded in. These values are SVY21, so 3414 is correct; passing 4326 (WGS84) would misproject everything.


I confirm the result is a POINT feature collection with the right CRS.

title: Hands-on Exercise 8: Geospatial Visualisation and Analytical Mapping with tmap
text:
3.4 Drawing a proportional symbol map
Proportional symbol maps work best interactively, so I switch tmap into view mode.


Show the code
tmap_mode("view")



3.4.1 Starting with a plain point map
tm_bubbles() draws fixed-size points. I set a constant fill, size, outline colour and line width.


Show the code
tm_shape(sgpools_sf) +
  tm_bubbles(fill = "red",
             size = 1,
             col = "black",
             lwd = 1)




3.4.2 Making the symbols proportional
To make the map proportional I assign a numeric field to size. Now each bubble’s area reflects its winnings.


Show the code
tm_shape(sgpools_sf) +
  tm_bubbles(fill = "red",
             size = "Gp1Gp2 Winnings",
             col = "black",
             lwd = 1)




3.4.3 Adding a colour dimension
I encode a second variable, OUTLET TYPE, into the fill colour, so the map shows both magnitude (size) and category (colour) at once.


Show the code
tm_shape(sgpools_sf) +
  tm_bubbles(fill = "OUTLET TYPE",
             size = "Gp1Gp2 Winnings",
             col = "black",
             lwd = 1)




3.4.4 Faceting with synchronised maps
A nice feature of view mode is that faceting still works, and sync = TRUE links the zoom and pan across panels so they always show the same extent.


Show the code
tm_shape(sgpools_sf) +
  tm_bubbles(fill = "OUTLET TYPE",
             size = "Gp1Gp2 Winnings",
             col = "black",
             lwd = 1) +
  tm_facets(by = "OUTLET TYPE",
            nrow = 1,
            sync = TRUE)


I switch back to plot mode before moving on, so the interactive viewer does not interfere with the static maps in Part C.


Show the code
tmap_mode("plot")








NoteMy takeaway on proportional symbols



Size and area encode quantity well, but I have to remember that humans underestimate area differences. A bubble that looks “twice as big” rarely reads as twice the value. The interactive view helps because I can hover for the exact number, but for a static map I would pair the bubbles with a clear size legend.

I start by mapping raw counts: total water points and functional water points, side by side.


Show the code
p1 <- tm_shape(NGA_wp) +
