text:
4.3 Choropleth maps for rates
Counts are misleading here because water points are not evenly distributed in space. An LGA with many functional points might simply be an LGA with many points overall. To map the topic of interest rather than raw size, I convert counts to proportions.


Show the code
NGA_wp <- NGA_wp %>%
  mutate(pct_functional = wp_functional / total_wp) %>%
  mutate(pct_nonfunctional = wp_nonfunctional / total_wp)


Now I map the rate of functional water points.


Show the code
tm_shape(NGA_wp) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "pct_functional",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "equal",
                n = 10,
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                position = c("right", "bottom"))) +
  tm_borders(lwd = 0.1,
             fill_alpha = 1) +
  tm_title("Rate map of functional water point by LGAs")















NoteMy takeaway on rates versus counts



This is the single most important idea in the whole exercise. Mapping counts answers “where are there many things”, which almost always just reproduces a population or density map. Mapping rates answers the question I actually care about, “where is the proportion high or low”. For any per-capita or per-total question, I now normalise before I map.

title: Hands-on Exercise 8: Geospatial Visualisation and Analytical Mapping with tmap
text:
4.4 Percentile map
A percentile map is a quantile map with six fixed categories: 0-1%, 1-10%, 10-50%, 50-90%, 90-99% and 99-100%. It is built to highlight the extremes at both tails. The breakpoints come from quantile() with an explicit cumulative probability vector, and both endpoints have to be included.

4.4.1 Data preparation
First I drop records with missing values, since they would break the quantile computation.


Show the code
NGA_wp <- NGA_wp %>%
  drop_na()


Then I build the percentile breakpoints. Note that I extract the variable with the geometry dropped, because base R functions like quantile() cannot handle the sticky geometry column.


Show the code
percent <- c(0, .01, .1, .5, .9, .99, 1)
var <- NGA_wp["pct_functional"] %>%
  st_set_geometry(NULL)
quantile(var[, 1], percent)


       0%        1%       10%       50%       90%       99%      100% 
0.0000000 0.0000000 0.2169811 0.4791667 0.8611111 1.0000000 1.0000000 








WarningGeometry travels with sf columns



When I subset a single column from an sf data frame, the geometry comes along for the ride. That is fine for mapping, but base R functions like quantile() choke on it. The fix is st_set_geometry(NULL), which strips the geometry and leaves a plain vector the maths can work with.




4.4.2 Why write a function
Rather than copy and paste the same mapping code for every variable, I write functions. The reasons are the same ones from R for Data Science: a named function documents intent, a single change propagates everywhere, and I stop introducing copy-paste mistakes like renaming a variable in one place but not another.


4.4.3 A helper to extract a clean vector
This small function pulls a named variable out of an sf data frame as a plain, unnamed vector.


Show the code
get.var <- function(vname, df) {
  v <- df[vname] %>%
    st_set_geometry(NULL)
  v <- unname(v[, 1])
  return(v)
}




4.4.4 The percentile mapping function
This wraps the whole percentile workflow: compute the breaks, then draw a two-layer map with custom labels.


Show the code
percentmap <- function(vnam, df, legtitle = NA, mtitle = "Percentile Map"){
  percent <- c(0, .01, .1, .5, .9, .99, 1)
  var <- get.var(vnam, df)
  bperc <- quantile(var, percent)
  tm_shape(df) +
    tm_polygons() +
  tm_shape(df) +
    tm_polygons(vnam,
                title = legtitle,
                breaks = bperc,
                palette = "Blues",
                labels = c("< 1%", "1% - 10%", "10% - 50%",
                           "50% - 90%", "90% - 99%", "> 99%")) +
    tm_borders() +
    tm_layout(main.title = mtitle,
              title.position = c("right", "bottom"))
}


I test it on total water points.


Show the code
percentmap("total_wp", NGA_wp)

title: Hands-on Exercise 8: Geospatial Visualisation and Analytical Mapping with tmap
text:
4.5 Box map
A box map is an augmented quartile map with two extra categories for the lower and upper outliers, exactly like the whiskers and points of a boxplot translated onto a map. The break logic has to handle whether outliers actually exist on each side.
I start by recalling what the boxplot of non-functional water points looks like.


Show the code
ggplot(data = NGA_wp,
       aes(x = "",
           y = wp_nonfunctional)) +
  geom_boxplot()










4.5.1 The boxbreaks function
This computes the seven break points. The tricky part is the conditional logic: when there are no lower outliers, the lowest break starts at the minimum value rather than the lower fence, and similarly for the upper side.


Show the code
boxbreaks <- function(v, mult = 1.5) {
  qv <- unname(quantile(v))
  iqr <- qv[4] - qv[2]
  upfence <- qv[4] + mult * iqr
  lofence <- qv[2] - mult * iqr
  # initialize break points vector
  bb <- vector(mode = "numeric", length = 7)
  # logic for lower and upper fences
  if (lofence < qv[1]) {  # no lower outliers
    bb[1] <- lofence
    bb[2] <- floor(qv[1])
  } else {
    bb[2] <- lofence
    bb[1] <- qv[1]
  }
  if (upfence > qv[5]) { # no upper outliers
    bb[7] <- upfence
    bb[6] <- ceiling(qv[5])
  } else {
    bb[6] <- upfence
    bb[7] <- qv[5]
  }
  bb[3:5] <- qv[2:4]
  return(bb)
}


I reuse the same get.var() helper from the percentile section.


Show the code
get.var <- function(vname, df) {
  v <- df[vname] %>% st_set_geometry(NULL)
  v <- unname(v[, 1])
  return(v)
}


I test the break logic on non-functional water points.


Show the code
var <- get.var("wp_nonfunctional", NGA_wp)
boxbreaks(var)


[1] -56.5   0.0  14.0  34.0  61.0 131.5 278.0




4.5.2 The boxmap function
Finally I wrap it all into a boxmap() function with six labelled classes, from lower outlier through the quartiles to upper outlier.


Show the code
boxmap <- function(vnam, df,
                   legtitle = NA,
                   mtitle = "Box Map",
                   mult = 1.5){
  var <- get.var(vnam, df)
  bb <- boxbreaks(var)
  tm_shape(df) +
    tm_polygons() +
  tm_shape(df) +
    tm_fill(vnam, title = legtitle,
            breaks = bb,
            palette = "Blues",
            labels = c("lower outlier",
                       "< 25%",
                       "25% - 50%",
                       "50% - 75%",
                       "> 75%",
                       "upper outlier")) +
    tm_borders() +
    tm_layout(main.title = mtitle,
              title.position = c("left", "top"))
}

tmap_mode("plot")
boxmap("wp_nonfunctional", NGA_wp)















NoteMy takeaway on extreme value maps



Percentile maps and box maps are exploratory data analysis brought onto the map. A normal quantile map hides outliers inside the top or bottom class, but these designs give outliers their own categories, so the LGAs that are genuinely unusual stand out instead of being averaged away. When my goal is to find anomalies rather than show the general pattern, these are the classifications I reach for.

title: Hands-on Exercise 6: Visualising and Analysing Network and Text Data
text:
This exercise is really about one idea: relationships. Up to now most of my charts have treated each observation as an isolated dot or bar. Here I finally get to visualise how things connect to each other.
I split the work into two halves that turn out to be more similar than they first look:

Network data (Part 1). I model two weeks of email traffic inside a company and study who talks to whom. The objects are people, and the connections are emails.
Text data (Part 2). I take a collection of newsgroup messages and study how words and documents relate. The objects are words and documents, and the connections come from co-occurrence and correlation.

The payoff is that both halves end up as the same kind of structure, a graph, and both lean on the same plotting engine, ggraph. So learning the network grammar once pays off twice.






TipThe workflow I keep reusing



For every visualisation in this course I follow the same loop: install packages, import data, wrangle into the right shape, build a basic version, then enhance and (where it helps) make it interactive. Networks add one extra mental step at the start: I have to decide what counts as a node and what counts as an edge before any plotting can begin.








ImportantData I need before rendering



This page reads from a data/ subfolder. To reproduce everything I made sure the following exist:
Part 1 (network):

data/GAStech_email_node.csv
data/GAStech_email_edge-v2.csv

Part 2 (text):

data/20news/ (a folder of newsgroup subfolders, each containing the raw message files)
data/rds/ (an empty folder, because I cache the combined text frame here with write_rds())

title: Hands-on Exercise 6: Visualising and Analysing Network and Text Data
text:
3.1 The data
The data set comes from an oil exploration company called GAStech. There are two files. The edges file records roughly 9,000 individual emails exchanged between 55 employees over two weeks. The nodes file lists each of those 55 employees with their name, department and job title.
The split into nodes and edges is itself the first lesson: a network is never one table, it is always two. One table answers “who exists” and the other answers “who is connected”.

title: Hands-on Exercise 6: Visualising and Analysing Network and Text Data
text:
3.2 Importing the data


Show the code
GAStech_nodes <- read_csv("data/GAStech_email_node.csv")
GAStech_edges <- read_csv("data/GAStech_email_edge-v2.csv")

text:
3.3 Reviewing and wrangling time
Before trusting any field I glimpse the edges to check the types.


Show the code

$ SentDate    <chr> "6/1/2014", "6/1/2014", "6/1/2014", "6/1/2014", "6/1/2014"…

$ targetLabel <chr> "Isak.Baza", "Lucas.Alcazar", "Felix.Resumir", "Hideki.Coc…








WarningThe trap I almost walked into



SentDate came in as a character string, not a date. If I had grouped or sorted by it without noticing, R would have treated dates alphabetically rather than chronologically, which silently breaks any time based analysis. Checking data types right after import is now a habit, not an afterthought.


I convert the date and derive the weekday. One small decision I made on purpose: I compute the weekday from the parsed SendDate column rather than from the raw character, so I am always working from a true date object.


Show the code
GAStech_edges <- GAStech_edges %>%
  mutate(SendDate = dmy(SentDate)) %>%
  mutate(Weekday = wday(SendDate,
                        label = TRUE,
                        abbr = FALSE))


Here dmy() reads the string as day, month, year and returns a real date, while wday() returns the weekday as an ordered factor. Keeping it ordered matters because Monday should sort before Friday, not alphabetically.

title: Hands-on Exercise 6: Visualising and Analysing Network and Text Data
text:
3.4 Aggregating the edges
The raw edges file has one row per email, which is far too granular to plot. Thousands of overlapping lines would be unreadable. So I aggregate: for each sender, receiver and weekday I count how many work related emails passed between them, and I keep only meaningful pairs.


Show the code
GAStech_edges_aggregated <- GAStech_edges %>%
  filter(MainSubject == "Work related") %>%
  group_by(source, target, Weekday) %>%
    summarise(Weight = n()) %>%
  filter(source != target) %>%
  filter(Weight > 1) %>%
  ungroup()


Three of these filters reflect deliberate analytical choices, not just cleaning. source != target removes self emails, Weight > 1 drops one off contacts so only repeated relationships survive, and the MainSubject filter keeps the analysis focused on work communication.

title: Hands-on Exercise 6: Visualising and Analysing Network and Text Data
section: 3.6 Plotting static network graphs with ggraph
text:
3.6 Plotting static network graphs with ggraph
ggraph is an extension of ggplot2, so the layered grammar I already know carries straight over. Every network graph has three moving parts: the nodes, the edges and the layout that decides where everything sits.
I start with the bare minimum: draw the edges as straight links and the nodes as points.


Show the code
ggraph(GAStech_graph) +
  geom_edge_link() +
  geom_node_point()





A first, deliberately plain network graph




The default ggplot2 theme keeps axes and gridlines, which make no sense for a network. theme_graph() strips all of that away.


Show the code
g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph) +
  geom_edge_link(aes()) +
  geom_node_point(aes())

g + theme_graph()









The layout is where networks differ most from ordinary charts, because there is no natural x and y. ggraph offers many algorithms. I use Fruchterman and Reingold (fr), a force directed layout that pushes connected nodes together and unconnected ones apart.


Show the code
g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph,
            layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes()) +
  geom_node_point(aes())

g + theme_graph()









A plain web of dots is hard to read, so I start mapping attributes to aesthetics. Colouring each node by department immediately reveals structure.


Show the code
g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph,
            layout = "nicely") +
  geom_edge_link(aes()) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = Department,
                      size = 3))

g + theme_graph()









Next I let the edges carry information too. Mapping line width to Weight shows which relationships are heavy, and a low alpha stops dense areas from turning into a solid blob.


Show the code
g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph,
            layout = "nicely") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(width = Weight),
                 alpha = 0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = Department),
                  size = 3)

g + theme_graph()















NoteMy takeaway on the grammar carrying over



This is the moment I appreciated learning the grammar of graphics properly in earlier exercises. Mapping Department to colour and Weight to width is exactly the same aes() thinking as before. The only new vocabulary is geom_edge_* and geom_node_* plus the dedicated scale_edge_width().

title: Hands-on Exercise 6: Visualising and Analysing Network and Text Data
text:
3.7 Faceting a network
Faceting is the network equivalent of small multiples, and it is genuinely useful here because it spreads a tangled graph across panels and reduces over plotting. ggraph gives three faceting verbs, and the difference between them is subtle but important.
Using facet_edges() I split by weekday. Nodes appear in every panel, but an edge only shows up in the panel of the day it belongs to.


Show the code
set_graph_style()

g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph,
            layout = "nicely") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(width = Weight),
                 alpha = 0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = Department),
                  size = 2) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

g + facet_edges(~Weekday)









Adding a frame around each panel makes the small multiples easier to read as separate units.


Show the code
g + facet_edges(~Weekday) +
  th_foreground(foreground = "grey80",
                border = TRUE)









Now facet_nodes(), which behaves differently. An edge is drawn only if both of its endpoints live in the same panel, so this view answers a different question: how does each department communicate internally.


Show the code
g + facet_nodes(~Department) +
  th_foreground(foreground = "grey80",
                border = TRUE)















WarningThe distinction that confused me at first



facet_edges() and facet_nodes() look almost identical in code but answer opposite questions. With facet_edges() I am slicing the connections by an edge attribute. With facet_nodes() I am slicing the actors and only keeping edges that stay inside a panel. Reading the panels wrongly would lead to completely wrong conclusions, so I now say the question out loud before choosing.

title: Hands-on Exercise 6: Visualising and Analysing Network and Text Data
text:
3.8 Network metrics analysis
Visual structure is suggestive, but I want numbers to back it up. Centrality measures rank how important each actor is to the network. There are several flavours, and here I use betweenness centrality, which is high for actors who sit on many shortest paths between others, in other words the brokers and bridges.
A nice feature from ggraph version 2 onward is that I can call a tidygraph algorithm directly inside aes() without precomputing it.


Show the code
g <- GAStech_graph %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(width = Weight),
                 alpha = 0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = Department,
                      size = centrality_betweenness()))

g + theme_graph()





Node size mapped to betweenness centrality

title: Hands-on Exercise 6: Visualising and Analysing Network and Text Data
text:
3.9 Visualising community
Beyond ranking individuals, I can ask whether the network breaks into natural groups. Community detection algorithms do exactly that. tidygraph inherits many from igraph, such as edge betweenness, Louvain, walktrap and label propagation. I start with edge betweenness.


Show the code
g <- GAStech_graph %>%
  mutate(community = as.factor(
    group_edge_betweenness(
      weights = Weight,
      directed = TRUE))) %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(
    aes(width = Weight),
    alpha = 0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(
    range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(
    aes(colour = community))

g + theme_graph()





Communities detected by edge betweenness




Colour alone leaves the group boundaries fuzzy, so I draw a hull around each community using geom_mark_hull() from ggforce. This time I detect communities with group_louvain() and also bring back betweenness to size the nodes.


Show the code
g <- GAStech_graph %>%
  activate(nodes) %>%
  convert(to_undirected) %>%
  mutate(community = as.factor(
    group_louvain(weights = Weight)),
         betweenness_measure = centrality_betweenness()) %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") +
  geom_mark_hull(
    aes(x, y,
        group = community,
        fill = community),
    alpha = 0.2,
    expand = unit(0.3, "cm"),
    radius = unit(0.3, "cm")
  ) +
  geom_edge_link(aes(width = Weight),
                 alpha = 0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(fill = Department,
                      size = betweenness_measure),
                      color = "black",
                      shape = 21)

g + theme_graph()





Communities outlined with convex hulls, node size by betweenness










NoteMy takeaway on metrics versus communities



These two ideas answer different questions and I try not to conflate them. Centrality is about individual importance, who the brokers are. Community detection is about group structure, which clusters naturally hold together. The hull plot is my favourite output of Part 1 because it layers both at once: the fill shows the groups, and the node size shows the brokers inside and between them.








WarningA practical note on group_optimal



group_optimal() is exact but can be slow and depends on the GLPK library being available. If it ever errors or hangs on a bigger graph, a fast and well behaved substitute is group_louvain(), which gives very similar groupings for this data.

title: Hands-on Exercise 6: Visualising and Analysing Network and Text Data
section: 3.10 Building an interactive network with visNetwork
text:
3.10 Building an interactive network with visNetwork
Static graphs are great for a report, but a network is something I genuinely want to poke at. visNetwork builds an interactive graph on top of the vis.js library, where I can drag nodes, zoom, and highlight neighbours.
It expects its own column names, so first I rebuild the aggregated edges with from and to id columns by joining the labels back to the node ids.


Show the code
GAStech_edges_aggregated <- GAStech_edges %>%
  left_join(GAStech_nodes, by = c("sourceLabel" = "label")) %>%
  rename(from = id) %>%
  left_join(GAStech_nodes, by = c("targetLabel" = "label")) %>%
  rename(to = id) %>%
  filter(MainSubject == "Work related") %>%
  group_by(from, to) %>%
    summarise(weight = n()) %>%
  filter(from != to) %>%
  filter(weight > 1) %>%
  ungroup()


The first interactive graph needs nothing more than the two tables.


Show the code
visNetwork(GAStech_nodes,
           GAStech_edges_aggregated)






I apply the familiar Fruchterman and Reingold layout, this time through igraph.


Show the code
visNetwork(GAStech_nodes,
           GAStech_edges_aggregated) %>%
  visIgraphLayout(layout = "layout_with_fr")






visNetwork automatically colours nodes by a column called group, so I rename Department to group to get a coloured, legible graph.


Show the code
GAStech_nodes <- GAStech_nodes %>%
  rename(group = Department)




Show the code
visNetwork(GAStech_nodes,
           GAStech_edges_aggregated) %>%
  visIgraphLayout(layout = "layout_with_fr") %>%
  visLegend() %>%
  visLayout(randomSeed = 123)






Because the graph is directed, I add arrowheads and a gentle curve to the edges.


Show the code
visNetwork(GAStech_nodes,
           GAStech_edges_aggregated) %>%
  visIgraphLayout(layout = "layout_with_fr") %>%
  visEdges(arrows = "to",
           smooth = list(enabled = TRUE,
                         type = "curvedCW")) %>%
  visLegend() %>%
  visLayout(randomSeed = 123)






Finally the part that makes it feel alive. visOptions() lets me highlight a node’s neighbours on click and adds a dropdown to jump straight to any person.


Show the code
visNetwork(GAStech_nodes,
           GAStech_edges_aggregated) %>%
  visIgraphLayout(layout = "layout_with_fr") %>%
  visOptions(highlightNearest = TRUE,
             nodesIdSelection = TRUE) %>%
  visLegend() %>%
  visLayout(randomSeed = 123)












NoteMy takeaway on static versus interactive



I now think of these as serving different readers. The ggraph versions are for a fixed narrative where I have already decided what matters and want to point at it. visNetwork is for an open ended audience who want to explore for themselves, click a name, and see who that person is connected to. One is a finished argument, the other is a tool for asking questions.

title: Hands-on Exercise 6: Visualising and Analysing Network and Text Data
text:
4.1 The tidytext idea
The central rule of tidytext is one token per row, where a token is usually a single word. Once text is in that shape, all the dplyr, tidyr and ggplot2 skills I already have apply directly. There is no separate text mining universe to learn, just a reshaping step at the front.

title: Hands-on Exercise 6: Visualising and Analysing Network and Text Data
section: 4.2 Importing many files from many folders
text:
4.2 Importing many files from many folders
The data is the classic 20 Newsgroups collection: many message files spread across folders, one folder per newsgroup. Reading them by hand is hopeless, so I write a small function that reads every file in one folder into a tidy frame.


Show the code
news20 <- "data/20news/"




Show the code
read_folder <- function(infolder) {
  tibble(file = dir(infolder,
                    full.names = TRUE)) %>%
    mutate(text = map(file,
                      read_lines)) %>%
    transmute(id = basename(file),
              text) %>%
    unnest(text)
}


Then I map that function over every folder, so a single pipeline ingests the entire corpus and labels each line with its newsgroup and message id. I cache the result so I do not have to repeat the slow read.


Show the code
raw_text <- tibble(folder =
                     dir(news20,
                         full.names = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(folder_out = map(folder,
                          read_folder)) %>%
  unnest(cols = c(folder_out)) %>%
  transmute(newsgroup = basename(folder),
            id, text)

write_rds(raw_text, "data/rds/news20.rds")








NoteMy takeaway on map and unnest



This little pipeline taught me more about functional programming than the network half did. map() applies my read_folder function to each folder and stores a whole data frame inside a list column, then unnest() flattens those frames back into ordinary rows. Writing one function and mapping it beats copying read code dozens of times, and it scales to any number of folders without edits.

title: Hands-on Exercise 6: Visualising and Analysing Network and Text Data
text:
4.3 Initial exploration
Before any cleaning I check the balance of the corpus by counting distinct messages per newsgroup.


Show the code
raw_text %>%
  group_by(newsgroup) %>%
  summarize(messages = n_distinct(id)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(messages, newsgroup)) +
  geom_col(fill = "lightblue") +
  labs(y = NULL)





Number of messages per newsgroup

title: Hands-on Exercise 6: Visualising and Analysing Network and Text Data
text:
4.4 Cleaning the text
Raw messages carry a lot of noise that would pollute any word count: headers, automated signatures, and quoted text from earlier messages. I remove them in two passes.
First I drop everything before the first blank line, which strips the header block, and I cut off anything after a signature line that starts with two dashes.


Show the code
cleaned_text <- raw_text %>%
  group_by(newsgroup, id) %>%
  filter(cumsum(text == "") > 0,
         cumsum(str_detect(
           text, "^--")) == 0) %>%
  ungroup()


Second I remove quoted lines, the ones that repeat what someone else wrote, using a few regular expressions.


Show the code
cleaned_text <- cleaned_text %>%
  filter(str_detect(text, "^[^>]+[A-Za-z\\d]")
         | text == "",
         !str_detect(text,
                     "writes(:|\\.\\.\\.)$"),
         !str_detect(text,
                     "^In article <")
  )








WarningCleaning is an analytical choice, not housekeeping



It is tempting to treat this as boring preprocessing, but every filter here shapes the conclusions. If I had left the headers in, words like “subject” and “from” would dominate every count and tell me nothing. If I had left quoted text in, popular opinions would be double counted because they get quoted back. Garbage in really does mean garbage out for text.

title: Hands-on Exercise 6: Visualising and Analysing Network and Text Data
text:
4.5 Tokenising and removing stop words
Now the key tidytext step. unnest_tokens() breaks each line into one word per row, and I then drop common stop words and anything that is not a clean word.


Show the code
usenet_words <- cleaned_text %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, text) %>%
  filter(str_detect(word, "[a-z']$"),
         !word %in% stop_words$word)


With clean tokens I can finally count the most common words across the whole corpus.


Show the code
usenet_words %>%
  count(word, sort = TRUE)


# A tibble: 5,542 × 2
   word           n
   <chr>      <int>
 1 people        57
 2 time          50
 3 jesus         47
 4 god           44
 5 message       40
 6 br            27
 7 bible         23
 8 drive         23
 9 homosexual    23
10 read          22
# ℹ 5,532 more rows


More useful for comparison is counting words within each newsgroup.


Show the code
words_by_newsgroup <- usenet_words %>%
  count(newsgroup, word, sort = TRUE) %>%
  ungroup()

title: Hands-on Exercise 6: Visualising and Analysing Network and Text Data
text:
4.6 Visualising words with word clouds
A word cloud is a quick, intuitive way to see prominence, where size encodes frequency. The base wordcloud package gives a fast static version.


Show the code
wordcloud(words_by_newsgroup$word,
          words_by_newsgroup$n,
          max.words = 300)





Word cloud of the corpus, size by frequency




A word cloud is good for a first impression but bad for reading exact values, so I pair it with an interactive DT table that lets me search and sort the actual numbers.


Show the code
words_by_newsgroup %>%
  slice_max(n, n = 500) %>%
  DT::datatable(filter = "top",
                options = list(pageLength = 10,
                               scrollX = TRUE))






I can also build the cloud inside ggplot2 with ggwordcloud, which means I get faceting for free and can show one small cloud per newsgroup.


Show the code
set.seed(1234)

words_by_newsgroup %>%
  filter(n > 0) %>%
  ggplot(aes(label = word,
             size = n)) +
  geom_text_wordcloud() +
  theme_minimal() +
  facet_wrap(~newsgroup)





Per newsgroup word clouds with ggwordcloud










NoteMy takeaway on word clouds



I used to think word clouds were just decoration, and honestly for precise reading they are weak. But as a first glance they are excellent, and pairing one with a searchable table covers both needs: the cloud for the gist, the table for the truth. The faceted ggwordcloud version is the one I would actually keep, because comparing clouds side by side says far more than one giant cloud.

title: Hands-on Exercise 6: Visualising and Analysing Network and Text Data
text:
4.7 Basic concept of TF-IDF
Plain frequency has a flaw: common words like “people” or “time” top every newsgroup and so distinguish none of them. TF-IDF, short for term frequency to inverse document frequency, fixes this by rewarding words that are frequent in one document but rare across the rest. A high TF-IDF word is therefore a word that is characteristic of a particular newsgroup.
bind_tf_idf() computes all three quantities and binds them to the data.


Show the code
tf_idf <- words_by_newsgroup %>%
  bind_tf_idf(word, newsgroup, n) %>%
  arrange(desc(tf_idf))


I present the result as an interactive table with rounded numbers and tighter rows.


Show the code
tf_idf %>%
  slice_max(tf_idf, n = 500) %>%
  DT::datatable(filter = "top",
                options = list(pageLength = 10,
                               scrollX = TRUE)) %>%
  formatRound(columns = c("tf", "idf",
                          "tf_idf"),
              digits = 3) %>%
  formatStyle(0,
              target = "row",
              lineHeight = "25%")






To see the payoff visually I use faceted bar charts of the top TF-IDF words for the science related newsgroups. The distinguishing vocabulary of each group jumps out.


Show the code
tf_idf %>%
  filter(str_detect(newsgroup, "^sci\\.")) %>%
  group_by(newsgroup) %>%
  slice_max(tf_idf,
            n = 12) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(word = reorder(word,
                        tf_idf)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(tf_idf,
             word,
             fill = newsgroup)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ newsgroup,
             scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "tf-idf",
       y = NULL)





Top TF-IDF words in the science newsgroups










NoteMy takeaway on why TF-IDF beats raw counts



This was the most useful concept in Part 2. Raw frequency tells me what is common, TF-IDF tells me what is distinctive, and distinctive is almost always what I actually want when comparing groups. Setting scales = "free" in the facet is a small but important detail, because each newsgroup has its own range and a shared axis would flatten the smaller ones into nothing.

title: Hands-on Exercise 6: Visualising and Analysing Network and Text Data
section: 4.8 From words to a network: correlations between newsgroups
text:
4.8 From words to a network: correlations between newsgroups
Here the two halves of this exercise finally meet. I can treat the newsgroups as nodes and connect ones that share similar vocabulary, turning a text problem back into a network problem. widyr makes this clean: it casts the tidy data into a wide matrix, computes pairwise correlations, then returns tidy output.


Show the code
newsgroup_cors <- words_by_newsgroup %>%
  filter(n >= 5) %>%
  pairwise_cor(newsgroup,
               word,
               n,
               sort = TRUE)


Now I draw the correlations as a network with ggraph, exactly the engine from Part 1, keeping only reasonably strong links.


Show the code
set.seed(2017)

newsgroup_cors %>%
  filter(correlation > .025) %>%
  graph_from_data_frame() %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(alpha = correlation,
                     width = correlation)) +
  geom_node_point(size = 6,
                  color = "lightblue") +
  geom_node_text(aes(label = name),
                 color = "red",
                 repel = TRUE) +
  theme_void()





Newsgroups connected by shared vocabulary










TipThe moment Part 1 and Part 2 connected



This plot is the whole point of putting both topics in one exercise. Nothing in the ggraph call is new, I reused everything from the email network, yet the underlying data is text. Realising that documents related by shared words are a network was the single most satisfying idea in this exercise.

title: Hands-on Exercise 6: Visualising and Analysing Network and Text Data
text:
4.9 Bigrams: relationships between words
So far I treated words as independent. But meaning lives in word order, so I now look at bigrams, pairs of consecutive words. unnest_tokens() handles this with a token type of ngrams.


Show the code
bigrams <- cleaned_text %>%
  unnest_tokens(bigram,
                text,
                token = "ngrams",
                n = 2)


A first count is dominated by uninformative pairs like “of the”, which is expected.


Show the code
bigrams_count <- bigrams %>%
  filter(bigram != "NA") %>%
  count(bigram, sort = TRUE)

bigrams_count

To get meaningful pairs I split each bigram into two columns and remove any pair containing a stop word.


Show the code
bigrams_separated <- bigrams %>%
  filter(bigram != "NA") %>%
  separate(bigram, c("word1", "word2"),
           sep = " ")

bigrams_filtered <- bigrams_separated %>%
  filter(!word1 %in% stop_words$word) %>%
  filter(!word2 %in% stop_words$word)

bigrams_filtered

Then I recount the cleaned word pairs.

bigram_counts <- bigrams_filtered %>%

text:
4.10 A network of bigrams
A bigram is itself a tiny directed edge from one word to the next, so the natural way to see them is a graph. I build it with graph_from_data_frame() from igraph, keeping only pairs that appear more than three times.


Show the code
bigram_graph <- bigram_counts %>%
  filter(n > 3) %>%
  graph_from_data_frame()

bigram_graph

+ edges from a6ae69e (vertex names):

A first plot shows the structure.


Show the code
set.seed(1234)

ggraph(bigram_graph, layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link() +
  geom_node_point() +
  geom_node_text(aes(label = name),
                 vjust = 1,
                 hjust = 1)





A first bigram network




I then polish it: arrowheads show reading direction, edge transparency encodes how often the pair occurs, and theme_void() clears the background so the words stand out.


Show the code

a <- grid::arrow(type = "closed",
                 length = unit(.15,
                               "inches"))

ggraph(bigram_graph,
       layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(edge_alpha = n),
                 show.legend = FALSE,
                 arrow = a,
                 end_cap = circle(.07,

  geom_node_text(aes(label = name),
                 vjust = 1,
                 hjust = 1) +

Bigram network with direction and frequency encoded










NoteMy takeaway on bigram networks



Seeing words drawn as a directed graph made an abstract idea concrete: language has structure, and that structure is a network. A chain like one word arrowing into the next is just an edge, which means the same betweenness and community tools from Part 1 could in principle run on words too. That symmetry is the lesson I am taking away from the whole exercise.

title: Hands-on Exercise 4: Seeing Distributions, Quantifying Uncertainty, Embedding Statistics, and Comparing Fairly
text:
This exercise covers four seemingly independent topics: visualising distributions, visualising uncertainty, visual statistical analysis, and funnel plots for fair comparison. At first I thought they had nothing to do with each other, but after working through them I realised they form a complete progression in how seriously we take a chart.
I reorganised the order based on my own understanding:
Step one, use ridgeline and raincloud plots to see the shape of the data clearly. This is the starting point of any analysis.
Step two, recognise that the sample mean is not the true mean. So we use error bars and ggdist to draw out how confident we actually are.
Step three, take it further by embedding the results of statistical tests (p values, effect sizes, Bayes factors) directly into the chart, so a single image performs both exploration and inference.
Step four, apply everything we have learned to a real problem: when sample sizes vary widely across entities (hospitals, schools, regions), how do we make a fair side-by-side comparison? That is what funnel plots are for.
By the end I realised these four chapters are not really four tools. They are a complete chain of thinking: from looking, to inferring, to comparing.

title: Hands-on Exercise 4: Seeing Distributions, Quantifying Uncertainty, Embedding Statistics, and Comparing Fairly
text:
1.1 Loading the Required Packages
Quite a few packages this time. I use pacman::p_load() to handle them all at once, and write the role of each one as a comment for future reference:

  ggridges,      # ridgeline / joyplots

  ggthemes,      # extra themes like economist
  colorspace,    # lighten / darken color helpers
  FunnelPlotR,   # funnel plot package
  plotly,        # interactive plots
  knitr,         # table rendering
  tidyverse      # data wrangling foundation
)

title: Hands-on Exercise 4: Seeing Distributions, Quantifying Uncertainty, Embedding Statistics, and Comparing Fairly
section: 2.1 Ridgeline Plot: Best Choice When You Have Many Groups
text:
2.1 Ridgeline Plot: Best Choice When You Have Many Groups
The essence of a ridgeline plot is stacking multiple distributions vertically with slight overlap, so you can compare many groups in a compact space.
Only consider it when you have 5 or more groups. With fewer groups, faceted density plots work better. Our CLASS variable has 9 classes, which is in the sweet spot.

2.1.1 Basic Ridgeline

ggplot(exam, 
       aes(x = ENGLISH, 
           y = CLASS)) +
  geom_density_ridges(
    scale = 3,
    rel_min_height = 0.01,
    bandwidth = 3.4,
    fill = lighten("#7097BB", .3),
    color = "white"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    name = "English Grades",
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  scale_y_discrete(name = NULL, 
                   expand = expansion(add = c(0.2, 2.6))) +
  theme_ridges()








How I think about the key parameters:
scale = 3 controls the height of each ridge. The larger the value, the chunkier the ridge and the more they overlap. I tried 1 and 5 and found 3 hits the sweet spot between “I can still see the shape of each ridge” and “the whole thing looks compact”.
rel_min_height = 0.01 cuts off the very low density tails. Without it you get long thin tails that are barely visible but still take up space.
bandwidth = 3.4 is the kernel density bandwidth. A small bandwidth gives a jagged curve, and a large one over-smooths and hides real structure.


2.1.2 Mapping Probability Information onto Color
Next level move: let the color carry information. The version below uses the empirical cumulative distribution function (ECDF) to compute the tail probability at each x position. The closer to the extremes, the darker the color.

ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = ENGLISH, 
           y = CLASS, 
           fill = 0.5 - abs(0.5 - after_stat(ecdf)))) +
  stat_density_ridges(geom = "density_ridges_gradient", 
                      calc_ecdf = TRUE) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Tail probability",
                       direction = -1) +
  theme_ridges()








A regular ridgeline only tells me what the distribution looks like for this class. The tail probability version tells me where any individual student sits within their own class. The dark areas are the extreme values (very high or very low) for that class.
Note that calc_ecdf = TRUE must be turned on, otherwise after_stat(ecdf) has no value to access. I forgot this the first time and spent a while debugging the error.


2.1.3 Coloring by Quartile
Another approach is to slice the distribution into quartiles and color each slice differently:

ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = ENGLISH, 
           y = CLASS, 
           fill = factor(after_stat(quantile)))) +
  stat_density_ridges(
    geom = "density_ridges_gradient",
    calc_ecdf = TRUE, 
    quantiles = 4,
    quantile_lines = TRUE) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(name = "Quartiles") +
  theme_ridges()








The biggest advantage of this version is that the median line is immediately visible (the boundary between the two middle slices). For “quickly comparing the central location across many groups”, this version beats the ECDF one.

title: Hands-on Exercise 4: Seeing Distributions, Quantifying Uncertainty, Embedding Statistics, and Comparing Fairly
section: 2.2 Raincloud Plot: Combining Boxplot, Density, and Dotplot in One
text:
2.2 Raincloud Plot: Combining Boxplot, Density, and Dotplot in One
Raincloud is named that way because it has three layers: the “cloud” on top (a half density), the “rain” in the middle (a boxplot), and the “rain drops” at the bottom (a dotplot). Three perspectives at once, each compensating for the others’ blind spots.

2.2.1 Layer One: Half-Eye

ggplot(exam, 
       aes(x = RACE, 
           y = ENGLISH)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5,
               justification = -0.2,
               .width = 0,
               point_colour = NA)








justification = -0.2 shifts the half density slightly to the right, leaving room for the boxplot we will add next. .width = 0 and point_colour = NA turn off the default “point + interval” decoration that ggdist adds by default, because at this layer I only want the density shape.


2.2.2 Layer Two: Boxplot

ggplot(exam, 
       aes(x = RACE, 
           y = ENGLISH)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5,
               justification = -0.2,
               .width = 0,
               point_colour = NA) +
  geom_boxplot(width = .20,
               outlier.shape = NA)








width = .20 squeezes the boxplot into a thin “needle” so it does not steal visual focus from the density. outlier.shape = NA hides the outliers, because the upcoming dotplot will draw all individual points anyway, so duplicate outlier marks are unnecessary.


2.2.3 Layer Three: Dotplot

ggplot(exam, 
       aes(x = RACE, 
           y = ENGLISH)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5,
               justification = -0.2,
               .width = 0,
               point_colour = NA) +
  geom_boxplot(width = .20,
               outlier.shape = NA) +
  stat_dots(side = "left", 
            justification = 1.2, 
            binwidth = NA,
            dotsize = 2)








side = "left" puts the dots on the left side, mirroring the density on the right. justification = 1.2 pushes them further left to avoid overlapping with the boxplot.


2.2.4 Final Polished Version
Flip the coordinates and apply a clean theme to get the classic horizontal raincloud:

ggplot(exam, 
       aes(x = RACE, 
           y = ENGLISH)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5,
               justification = -0.2,
               .width = 0,
               point_colour = NA) +
  geom_boxplot(width = .20,
               outlier.shape = NA) +
  stat_dots(side = "left", 
            justification = 1.2, 
            binwidth = NA,
            dotsize = 1.5) +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_economist()

title: Hands-on Exercise 4: Seeing Distributions, Quantifying Uncertainty, Embedding Statistics, and Comparing Fairly
text:
2.3 Wrap-up of Part 1
Ridgeline and raincloud look complex, but they both solve the same underlying problem: boxplots have too low information density.
Ridgeline is great for “quick comparison across many groups”, and raincloud is great for “deep dive into a single group”. For my future projects, I will reach for ridgeline when comparing 5 or more groups, and raincloud when looking at 2 to 4 groups in detail.

title: Hands-on Exercise 4: Seeing Distributions, Quantifying Uncertainty, Embedding Statistics, and Comparing Fairly
section: 3.1 Manually Drawing Error Bars with ggplot2
text:
3.1 Manually Drawing Error Bars with ggplot2
The classic approach. First use dplyr to compute the mean, standard deviation, and standard error for each group:

my_sum <- exam %>%
  group_by(RACE) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean = mean(MATHS),
    sd = sd(MATHS)
  ) %>%
  mutate(se = sd / sqrt(n - 1))

How I think about these statistics: standard deviation (sd) describes how spread out the data itself is. Standard error (se) describes how uncertain we are about the mean estimate. These two are often confused. The formula for se is sd divided by sqrt(n), which means the larger the sample, the more precise our estimate of the mean, and the smaller the se.

3.1.1 Standard Error Bars

ggplot(my_sum) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(x = RACE, 
        ymin = mean - se,

3.1.2 95% Confidence Intervals
Replace ±1 SE with ±1.96 SE to get the 95% confidence interval. I also added reorder() to sort by mean, which makes the chart easier to read:

  geom_errorbar(
    aes(x = reorder(RACE, -mean), 
        ymin = mean - 1.96*se, 
        ymax = mean + 1.96*se), 
    width = 0.2, 
    colour = "black", 
    alpha = 0.9, 
    linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(aes(x = RACE, 
                 y = mean), 
             stat = "identity", 
             color = "red",
             size = 1.5,
             alpha = 1) +
  labs(x = "Race",
       y = "Mean Maths Score",
       title = "95% Confidence Interval of Mean Maths Score by Race")








The trick to reading this chart: if two groups’ confidence intervals do not overlap, their means are almost certainly significantly different; if they overlap heavily, the difference is likely not significant. This is a much smarter visual judgement than just eyeballing bar heights.

text:
3.2 Doing It Elegantly with ggdist
The ggdist package offers a much cleaner syntax. No need to compute summaries manually.

3.2.1 stat_pointinterval: Auto-Compute Intervals

exam %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = RACE, y = MATHS)) +
  stat_pointinterval() +
  labs(
    title = "Multiple Confidence Intervals of Mean Maths Score",
    subtitle = "Default shows 66% and 95% intervals")








ggdist by default draws two layers of lines with different thicknesses, representing the 66% and 95% intervals. This multiple intervals in one chart design carries more information than a single interval.


3.2.2 Customising the Intervals
If we only want the 95% interval and switch the point to median:

exam %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = RACE, y = MATHS)) +
  stat_pointinterval(.width = 0.95,
                     .point = median,
                     .interval = qi) +
  labs(
    title = "95% Interval of Median Maths Score",
    subtitle = "Median is more robust to outliers than mean")








I noticed that ggdist treats mean and median as first-class citizens equally. When the data is skewed or has outliers, median is more reliable than mean. Being able to swap so easily is a big advantage of ggdist.


3.2.3 Showing Multiple Confidence Levels at Once

exam %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = RACE, y = MATHS)) +
  stat_pointinterval(
    .width = c(0.95, 0.99),
    show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Showing 95% and 99% Intervals Simultaneously",
    subtitle = "Outer thick line = 95%, inner thin line = 99%")










3.2.4 Gradient Interval Plot (Prettier and More Honest)

exam %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = RACE, y = MATHS)) +
  stat_gradientinterval(   
    fill = "skyblue",      
    show.legend = TRUE     
  ) +                        
  labs(
    title = "Gradient-Style Uncertainty Visualisation",
    subtitle = "Darker areas indicate higher probability of the estimate")








Why I think this gradient design is great: it removes the binary “inside vs outside the interval” split. Traditional error bars make people feel “every value inside the interval is equally likely”, but the truth is that values closer to the center are more likely. The gradient version is more honest about that.

Core idea of uncertainty visualisation: every point estimate should come with its uncertainty information. Otherwise we are deceiving the reader.
Manual error bars give precise control over every detail and are great for publication-ready charts. ggdist’s one-liner is better for exploratory analysis. I will keep both tools in my toolkit and pick based on the situation.

text:
4.1 One-Sample Test: gghistostats
Suppose we want to test whether the mean English score across all students equals 60. The traditional workflow is to run a t-test, then draw a histogram, then verbally explain the result. gghistostats collapses all three into one:

set.seed(1234)

gghistostats(
  data = exam,
  x = ENGLISH,
  type = "bayes",
  test.value = 60,
  xlab = "English Scores"
)








The information density in the title area is enormous. What appears here is BF₁₀, the Bayes factor. It tells us the strength of evidence in favor of the alternative hypothesis relative to the strength of evidence in favor of the null.
My quick reference for interpreting Bayes factors (based on Jeffreys 1961, revised by Lee & Wagenmakers 2013):



BF₁₀ Range
Interpretation




> 100
Extreme evidence for H₁


30 to 100
Very strong evidence for H₁


10 to 30
Strong evidence for H₁


3 to 10
Moderate evidence for H₁


1 to 3
Anecdotal evidence for H₁


1
No evidence for either


1/3 to 1
Anecdotal evidence for H₀


1/10 to 1/3
Moderate evidence for H₀



The advantage of Bayes factors over p values: they are symmetric. They can quantify both “evidence for H₀” and “evidence for H₁”, whereas p values can only reject H₀ but cannot “accept H₀”.

4.2 Two-Sample Mean Test: ggbetweenstats
Comparing maths scores between male and female students:

ggbetweenstats(
  data = exam,
  x = GENDER, 
  y = MATHS,
  type = "np",
  messages = FALSE
)








type = "np" means using a non-parametric test (Mann Whitney U). When the data does not satisfy normality assumptions, non-parametric tests are safer.

4.3 One-Way ANOVA: Still ggbetweenstats
Switch the grouping variable from binary to multi-class (RACE), and add pairwise comparisons:

ggbetweenstats(
  data = exam,
  x = RACE, 
  y = ENGLISH,
  type = "p",
  mean.ci = TRUE, 
  pairwise.comparisons = TRUE, 
  pairwise.display = "s",
  p.adjust.method = "fdr",
  messages = FALSE
)








Parameter notes (these are things I had to dig into the docs to figure out):
pairwise.display = "s" only shows pairwise comparisons that are statistically significant, avoiding a chart cluttered with “ns” (not significant) labels.
p.adjust.method = "fdr" uses the False Discovery Rate method to correct p values for multiple comparisons. Not correcting for multiple comparisons inflates the false positive rate dramatically. FDR is one of the most popular correction methods today.

4.5 Contingency Table Test of Association: ggbarstats
First slice maths scores into 4 bins (poor, fair, good, excellent):

exam1 <- exam %>% 
  mutate(MATHS_bins = 
           cut(MATHS, 
               breaks = c(0, 60, 75, 85, 100)))

Then test whether “maths score bin” is independent of “gender”:

ggbarstats(exam1, 
           x = MATHS_bins, 
           y = GENDER)








This is a chi-square test of independence visualised. If the p value is significant, it means male and female students are distributed differently across score bins.

text:
5.4 Building One from Scratch with ggplot2
The best way to understand the principle of a funnel plot is to build one by hand. Step one, compute the rate and standard error for each point:

df <- covid19 %>%
  mutate(rate = Death / Positive) %>%
  mutate(rate.se = sqrt((rate * (1 - rate)) / Positive)) %>%
  filter(rate > 0)

rate.se uses the binomial standard error formula sqrt(p(1-p)/n). This formula is crucial. It explains why the funnel narrows as n grows: larger n means larger denominator, smaller se, and a tighter “reasonable range”.
Step two, compute the overall weighted average rate across all entities, used as the funnel’s centerline:

fit.mean <- weighted.mean(df$rate, 1 / df$rate.se^2)
fit.mean

[1] 0.01496959


Notice the weight is 1/se^2, which is inverse-variance weighting. This is the standard practice in meta-analysis. The idea is “the more precise the estimate, the higher its weight”.
Step three, generate the upper and lower bound curves for 95% and 99.9%:

number.seq <- seq(1, max(df$Positive), 1)
number.ll95 <- fit.mean - 1.96 * sqrt((fit.mean*(1-fit.mean)) / number.seq) 
number.ul95 <- fit.mean + 1.96 * sqrt((fit.mean*(1-fit.mean)) / number.seq) 
number.ll999 <- fit.mean - 3.29 * sqrt((fit.mean*(1-fit.mean)) / number.seq) 
number.ul999 <- fit.mean + 3.29 * sqrt((fit.mean*(1-fit.mean)) / number.seq) 

dfCI <- data.frame(number.ll95, number.ul95, number.ll999, 
                   number.ul999, number.seq, fit.mean)

1.96 corresponds to two-sided 95%, and 3.29 corresponds to two-sided 99.8% (also known as the 3 sigma rule).
Step four, draw the chart:

p <- ggplot(df, aes(x = Positive, y = rate)) +
  geom_point(aes(label = `Sub-district`), 
             alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_line(data = dfCI, 
            aes(x = number.seq, y = number.ll95), 
            size = 0.4, colour = "grey40", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(data = dfCI, 
            aes(x = number.seq, y = number.ul95), 
            size = 0.4, colour = "grey40", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(data = dfCI, 
            aes(x = number.seq, y = number.ll999), 
            size = 0.4, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(data = dfCI, 
            aes(x = number.seq, y = number.ul999), 
            size = 0.4, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_hline(data = dfCI, 
             aes(yintercept = fit.mean), 
             size = 0.4, colour = "grey40") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 0.05)) +
  annotate("text", x = 1, y = -0.13, label = "95%", size = 3, colour = "grey40") + 
  annotate("text", x = 4.5, y = -0.18, label = "99%", size = 3, colour = "grey40") + 
  ggtitle("Cumulative Fatality Rate by Cumulative Number of COVID-19 Cases") +
  xlab("Cumulative Number of COVID-19 Cases") + 
  ylab("Cumulative Fatality Rate") +
  theme_light() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 12),
        legend.position = c(0.91, 0.85), 
        legend.title = element_text(size = 7),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 7),
        legend.background = element_rect(colour = "grey60", linetype = "dotted"),
        legend.key.height = unit(0.3, "cm"))
p

3. Beyond ggplot2 Annotation: ggrepel
When plotting a scatterplot with many data points, adding labels using geom_label() or geom_text() often results in overlapping text that is difficult to read.

3.1 The Problem: Overlapping Labels


Show code
ggplot(exam_data,
       aes(x = MATHS, y = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = lm, linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_label(aes(label = ID),
             hjust = 0.5,
             vjust = -0.5) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 100),
                  ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(title = "English scores versus Maths scores for Primary 3",
       x = "Maths Score", y = "English Score") +
  theme_minimal()











3.2 The Solution: ggrepel
ggrepel solves this by automatically adjusting label positions to avoid overlap. Simply replace:

geom_label() → geom_label_repel()
geom_text() → geom_text_repel()



Show code
ggplot(exam_data,
       aes(x = MATHS, y = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = lm, linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_label_repel(aes(label = ID),
                   fontface = "bold",
                   max.overlaps = 20) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 100),
                  ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(title = "English scores versus Maths scores for Primary 3",
       x = "Maths Score", y = "English Score") +
  theme_minimal()

  theme_classic()







theme_gray() — default







theme_classic()

theme_economist()







theme_wsj()

text:
5. Beyond Single Graph: patchwork
In data storytelling, a single chart is rarely sufficient. patchwork allows us to combine multiple ggplot2 plots into one cohesive composite figure using simple, intuitive operators.

5.1 Creating the Individual Plots
We first create three plots separately and store them as objects:


Show code
p1 <- ggplot(exam_data, aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 boundary = 100,
                 color = "grey25",
                 fill = "grey90") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Maths Scores") +
  theme_minimal()

p2 <- ggplot(exam_data, aes(x = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 boundary = 100,
                 color = "grey25",
                 fill = "grey90") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of English Scores") +
  theme_minimal()

p3 <- ggplot(exam_data,
             aes(x = MATHS, y = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = lm, linewidth = 0.5) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 100),
                  ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(title = "English vs Maths Scores",
       x = "Maths Score", y = "English Score") +
  theme_minimal()




5.2 Two-Column Layout: +
The + operator places two plots side by side:


Show code
p1 + p2











5.3 Three-Plot Composite Layout
Using a combination of / (stack vertically) and | (place side by side):


Show code
(p1 / p2) | p3











5.4 Adding Tags to Subplots
plot_annotation() automatically labels each subplot, making it easy to reference them in text:


Show code
((p1 / p2) | p3) +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "I")











5.5 Inset Plot
inset_element() allows you to embed a smaller plot inside a larger one, useful for showing a zoomed-in view or a supplementary chart:


Show code
p3 + inset_element(p2,
                   left = 0.02,
                   bottom = 0.7,
                   right = 0.5,
                   top = 1)











5.6 Combining patchwork with ggthemes
The & operator applies a theme to all plots in a patchwork composite simultaneously:


Show code
patchwork <- (p1 / p2) | p3
patchwork & theme_economist()















Note



Notice the difference between + and & in patchwork:

+ adds elements to the last plot only
& applies the element to all plots in the composite

text:
6. Key Takeaways
This exercise let me learn how ggplot2 extensions can significantly elevate the quality of statistical graphics:

ggrepel solves the overlapping label problem automatically — always prefer geom_label_repel() over geom_label() when labelling individual data points
ggthemes provides ready-made publication themes that immediately give your plots a professional appearance
hrbrthemes is particularly useful when typography and readability are a priority
patchwork makes it easy to tell a multi-panel visual story with minimal code — use / to stack, | to place side by side, and & to apply themes globally
Composite figures with plot_annotation(tag_levels = "I") are especially important in academic writing where subplots need to be referenced in text

text:
This exercise explores the foundational principles of ggplot2, an R package for declaratively creating data-driven graphics based on Leland Wilkinson’s Grammar of Graphics. Unlike Base R graphics which relies on a series of function calls, ggplot2 adopts a structured layered approach that makes visualisations more readable, reproducible, and aesthetically consistent.
The key idea behind ggplot2 can be summarised as:

“The transferable skills from ggplot2 are not the idiosyncrasies of plotting syntax, but a powerful way of thinking about visualisation, as a way of mapping between variables and the visual properties of geometric objects that you can perceive.” — Hadley Wickham

“The transferable skills from ggplot2 are not the idiosyncrasies of plotting syntax, but a powerful way of thinking about visualisation, as a way of mapping between variables and the visual properties of geometric objects that you can perceive.” — Hadley Wickham

title: Hands-on Exercise 1: A Layered Grammar of Graphics
text:
3. The Grammar of Graphics
ggplot2 builds every plot from seven layered components. Understanding these components is essential to constructing meaningful visualisations.







Component
Role




Data
The dataset being plotted


Aesthetics
Maps data variables to visual properties (position, colour, size, shape)


Geometrics
The visual marks used to represent data (points, bars, lines)


Facets
Splits data into subplots by a categorical variable


Statistics
Applies statistical transformations (mean, confidence intervals)


Coordinates
Defines the plane on which data is mapped


Themes
Controls non-data elements such as background and fonts



A plot is built by stacking these layers using the + operator.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1: A Layered Grammar of Graphics
text:
4. Base R Graphics vs ggplot2
To appreciate the advantages of ggplot2, it is useful to compare it with Base R graphics using the same dataset.

Show code
# Base R
hist(exam_data$MATHS,
     main = "Distribution of Maths Scores",
     xlab = "Maths Score",
     col = "grey80")
# ggplot2
ggplot(exam_data, aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 fill = "steelblue",
                 color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Maths Scores",
       x = "Maths Score",
       y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()







Base R: hist()







ggplot2: geom_histogram()





While Base R offers a quick way to produce plots, ggplot2 provides a more systematic and extensible framework, especially when dealing with complex multi-layered visualisations.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1: A Layered Grammar of Graphics
text:
5. Essential Geometric Objects
Geometric objects (geoms) define what type of mark is drawn on the plot. Below are the key geoms introduced in this exercise.

5.1 Bar Chart — geom_bar()
Used to visualise the frequency of a categorical variable.


Show code
ggplot(exam_data, aes(x = RACE)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Number of Students by Race",
       x = "Race", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()











5.2 Dot Plot — geom_dotplot()
Each dot represents one observation. Useful for small datasets to see individual data points.


Show code
ggplot(exam_data, aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot(binwidth = 2.5,
               dotsize = 0.5,
               fill = "steelblue") +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL, breaks = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Dot Plot of Maths Scores",
       x = "Maths Score") +
  theme_minimal()















Note



The y-axis is suppressed here as it does not carry meaningful information in a dot plot.




5.3 Histogram — geom_histogram()
Used to visualise the distribution of a continuous variable.

Show code
ggplot(exam_data, aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 fill = "steelblue",
                 color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Maths Score Distribution",
       x = "Maths Score", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()
ggplot(exam_data, aes(x = MATHS, fill = GENDER)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 color = "grey30") +
  labs(title = "Maths Score Distribution by Gender",
       x = "Maths Score", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()







Default histogram







Coloured by gender







5.4 Kernel Density Plot — geom_density()
A smoothed version of the histogram, useful for visualising the underlying distribution.


Show code
ggplot(exam_data, aes(x = MATHS, colour = GENDER)) +
  geom_density(linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Kernel Density Estimate of Maths Scores by Gender",
       x = "Maths Score", y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal()











5.5 Boxplot — geom_boxplot()
Displays the five-number summary (minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum) and highlights outliers.

Show code
ggplot(exam_data, aes(x = GENDER, y = MATHS)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(title = "Maths Scores by Gender",
       x = "Gender", y = "Maths Score") +
  theme_minimal()
ggplot(exam_data, aes(x = GENDER, y = MATHS)) +
  geom_boxplot(notch = TRUE,
               fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(title = "Notched Boxplot of Maths Scores by Gender",
       x = "Gender", y = "Maths Score") +
  theme_minimal()







Standard boxplot







Notched boxplot











Tip



If the notches of two boxplots do not overlap, there is strong evidence that their medians differ.




5.6 Violin Plot — geom_violin()
Combines a boxplot with a kernel density estimate, showing both summary statistics and the full distribution shape.


Show code
ggplot(exam_data, aes(x = GENDER, y = MATHS)) +
  geom_violin(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(title = "Violin Plot of Maths Scores by Gender",
       x = "Gender", y = "Maths Score") +
  theme_minimal()











5.7 Scatterplot — geom_point()
Used to visualise the relationship between two continuous variables.


Show code
ggplot(exam_data, aes(x = MATHS, y = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, colour = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Maths vs English Scores",
       x = "Maths Score", y = "English Score") +
  theme_minimal()











5.8 Combining Geoms
Multiple geoms can be layered on the same plot using +.


Show code
ggplot(exam_data, aes(x = GENDER, y = MATHS)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_point(position = "jitter",
             size = 0.5,
             alpha = 0.4,
             colour = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Boxplot with Jittered Data Points",
       x = "Gender", y = "Maths Score") +
  theme_minimal()

text:
6. Statistical Transformations
Statistical functions (stat_*) allow us to overlay computed summaries on top of raw data.

6.1 Adding Mean to Boxplot

Show code
ggplot(exam_data, aes(x = GENDER, y = MATHS)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  stat_summary(geom = "point",
               fun = "mean",
               colour = "red",
               size = 4) +
  labs(title = "stat_summary() method",
       x = "Gender", y = "Maths Score") +
  theme_minimal()
ggplot(exam_data, aes(x = GENDER, y = MATHS)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_point(stat = "summary",
             fun = "mean",
             colour = "red",
             size = 4) +
  labs(title = "geom_point(stat = 'summary') method",
       x = "Gender", y = "Maths Score") +
  theme_minimal()







Using stat_summary()







Using geom_point(stat = ‘summary’)







6.2 Best Fit Curve — geom_smooth()

Show code
ggplot(exam_data, aes(x = MATHS, y = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "LOESS Smoothing",
       x = "Maths Score", y = "English Score") +
  theme_minimal()
ggplot(exam_data, aes(x = MATHS, y = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = lm, linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Linear Model",
       x = "Maths Score", y = "English Score") +
  theme_minimal()







LOESS smoothing (default)







Linear model

title: Hands-on Exercise 1: A Layered Grammar of Graphics
text:
7. Facets
Facets generate small multiples — the same plot repeated across subsets of data. This is particularly useful for comparing distributions across groups.

7.1 facet_wrap()
Wraps panels into a 2D grid, ideal for a single grouping variable.


Show code
ggplot(exam_data, aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 fill = "steelblue",
                 color = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ CLASS) +
  labs(title = "Maths Score Distribution by Class",
       x = "Maths Score", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()











7.2 facet_grid()
Forms a matrix of panels defined by two grouping variables.


Show code
ggplot(exam_data, aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 fill = "steelblue",
                 color = "white") +
  facet_grid(~ CLASS) +
  labs(title = "Maths Score Distribution by Class (facet_grid)",
       x = "Maths Score", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()

title: Hands-on Exercise 1: A Layered Grammar of Graphics
text:
8. Coordinates
Coordinate systems control how data is mapped onto the 2D plane of the plot.

8.1 coord_flip()
Flips the x and y axes — useful for horizontal bar charts with long category labels.

Show code
ggplot(exam_data, aes(x = RACE)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Default: Vertical",
       x = "Race", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()
ggplot(exam_data, aes(x = RACE)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Flipped: Horizontal",
       x = "Race", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()







Vertical bar chart (default)







Horizontal bar chart (coord_flip)







8.2 coord_cartesian() — Fixing Axis Ranges
Setting equal axis ranges ensures scatterplots are not visually misleading.

Show code
ggplot(exam_data, aes(x = MATHS, y = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = lm, linewidth = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "Default Axis Range",
       x = "Maths Score", y = "English Score") +
  theme_minimal()
ggplot(exam_data, aes(x = MATHS, y = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = lm, linewidth = 0.5) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 100), ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(title = "Fixed Axis Range (0–100)",
       x = "Maths Score", y = "English Score") +
  theme_minimal()







Default axis range







Fixed axis range (0–100)

title: Hands-on Exercise 1: A Layered Grammar of Graphics
text:
9. Themes
Themes control the non-data elements of a plot: background colour, grid lines, font sizes, and axis labels.

Show code
ggplot(exam_data, aes(x = RACE)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "theme_gray()") +
  theme_gray()
ggplot(exam_data, aes(x = RACE)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "theme_classic()") +
  theme_classic()
ggplot(exam_data, aes(x = RACE)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "theme_minimal()") +
  theme_minimal()







theme_gray() — default







theme_classic()







theme_minimal()











Tip



theme_minimal() is generally preferred in academic and data journalism contexts as it reduces visual clutter and keeps the focus on the data.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1: A Layered Grammar of Graphics
text:
10. Key Takeaways
This exercise demonstrates that ggplot2’s layered grammar provides a principled and flexible framework for building statistical graphics. The key insights are:

Start with data and aesthetics — define what variables map to which visual properties
Choose the right geom — different geoms suit different data types and analytical goals
Layer deliberately — combining geoms (e.g. boxplot + jitter) reveals more information than either alone
Use facets for comparison — small multiples are more effective than overloaded single plots
Apply statistical summaries — overlaying means or trend lines adds analytical value
Fix axis ranges — always set equal axis limits when comparing two variables on the same scale
Choose themes purposefully — theme_minimal() or theme_classic() are generally preferred for clean, publication-ready visuals
