title: Hands-on Exercise 3: Programming Interactive Data Visualisation with R
text:
The core idea of this exercise is to make “static charts come alive”. In the previous two assignments, I learned how to create various statistical plots with ggplot2, but those charts were always “look-once-and-done” , readers could only passively accept the perspective I gave them. This time, I want to turn readers from passive observers into active explorers.
Specifically, I want to achieve three goals through this exercise:

Understand the “grammar” of interactivity: ggiraph abstracts interactive behaviors through three arguments, tooltip / data_id / onclick. This is actually a very elegant design philosophy.
Master two technical paths: ggiraph extends ggplot2, while plotly is an independent interactive engine.
Learn to build Coordinated Multiple Views: This is the most valuable part of interactive visualisation

title: Hands-on Exercise 3: Programming Interactive Data Visualisation with R
text:
1.1 Loading Required R Packages
The code chunk below uses pacman::p_load() to check, install, and load all required packages in one go. I prefer this over the traditional library() approach because it saves the trouble of writing one line per package.

pacman::p_load(ggiraph, plotly, 
               patchwork, DT, tidyverse, crosstalk) 

My understanding of each package:

ggiraph: “Translates” ggplot charts into SVG, then injects interactive behaviors
plotly: An independent interactive plotting system based on plotly.js
DT: Renders R data frames as searchable, sortable HTML tables
crosstalk: Allows different htmlwidgets to “talk” to each other (linked filtering)
patchwork: A handy tool for combining multiple ggplots into one figure
tidyverse: The fundamental toolkit

title: Hands-on Exercise 3: Programming Interactive Data Visualisation with R
text:
1.2 Importing the Data

exam_data <- read_csv("data/Exam_data.csv")

The dataset contains exam results of 322 students, including ID, class, gender, race, and scores in English, Maths, and Science.

glimpse(exam_data)

Rows: 322
Columns: 7
$ ID      <chr> "Student321", "Student305", "Student289", "Student227", "Stude…
$ CLASS   <chr> "3I", "3I", "3H", "3F", "3I", "3I", "3I", "3I", "3I", "3H", "3…
$ GENDER  <chr> "Male", "Female", "Male", "Male", "Male", "Female", "Male", "M…
$ RACE    <chr> "Malay", "Malay", "Chinese", "Chinese", "Malay", "Malay", "Chi…
$ ENGLISH <dbl> 21, 24, 26, 27, 27, 31, 31, 31, 33, 34, 34, 36, 36, 36, 37, 38…
$ MATHS   <dbl> 9, 22, 16, 77, 11, 16, 21, 18, 19, 49, 39, 35, 23, 36, 49, 30,…
$ SCIENCE <dbl> 15, 16, 16, 31, 25, 16, 25, 27, 15, 37, 42, 22, 32, 36, 35, 45…


My observation: The data is very “clean” with no missing values. CLASS is a categorical variable (string), and the three subject scores are numeric. This structure is well-suited for demonstrating interactive visualisation, there are continuous variables for scatter/histogram plots, and categorical variables for highlighting groups.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3: Programming Interactive Data Visualisation with R
text:
2.1 Basic Tooltip Usage
The simplest interaction — display data point information when the mouse hovers over it:

p <- ggplot(data = exam_data, 
            aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(
    aes(tooltip = ID),          # Key: use ID as tooltip content
    stackgroups = TRUE, 
    binwidth = 1, 
    method = "histodot") +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL, 
                     breaks = NULL)

girafe(
  ggobj = p,
  width_svg = 6,
  height_svg = 6 * 0.618    # Golden ratio — looks more pleasant
)





My thoughts: Notice that we’re using geom_dotplot_interactive() here, not the regular geom_dotplot(). ggiraph provides _interactive versions for almost all common geoms. The benefit of this design is — almost zero learning cost for ggplot users. You only need to change geom_xxx to geom_xxx_interactive.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3: Programming Interactive Data Visualisation with R
section: 2.2 Displaying More Information in the Tooltip
text:
2.2 Displaying More Information in the Tooltip
Showing only the ID is too sparse. In real-world scenarios, we often want to see a “mini profile” of the data point on hover. The trick is to first concatenate a new field in the data:

exam_data$tooltip <- c(paste0(     
  "Student ID: ", exam_data$ID,         
  "\nClass: ", exam_data$CLASS,
  "\nMaths Score: ", exam_data$MATHS)) 

p <- ggplot(data = exam_data, 
            aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(
    aes(tooltip = exam_data$tooltip), 
    stackgroups = TRUE,
    binwidth = 1,
    method = "histodot") +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,               
                     breaks = NULL)

girafe(
  ggobj = p,
  width_svg = 8,
  height_svg = 8 * 0.618
)





My thoughts: \n is used for line breaks, meaning the tooltip is essentially treated as plain text. At first I thought I’d need HTML tags, but it turns out a simple newline character is enough. For richer formatting (bold, colours), you need the CSS customisation in the next section.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3: Programming Interactive Data Visualisation with R
text:
2.3 Customising Tooltip Style
The default tooltip looks rather “plain” black background, white text, no character. With CSS we can give it a complete makeover:

tooltip_css <- "background-color: #fff8e1;
                color: #333;
                font-family: 'Helvetica Neue', sans-serif;
                padding: 8px 12px;
                border-radius: 6px;
                border: 1px solid #ffc107;
                box-shadow: 0 2px 8px rgba(0,0,0,0.15);"

p <- ggplot(data = exam_data, 
            aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(              
    aes(tooltip = ID),                   
    stackgroups = TRUE,                  
    binwidth = 1,                        
    method = "histodot") +               
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,               
                     breaks = NULL)

girafe(                                  
  ggobj = p,                             
  width_svg = 6,                         
  height_svg = 6 * 0.618,
  options = list(    
    opts_tooltip(    
      css = tooltip_css))
)                                        





My thoughts: Compared to the “black-and-white bold” style in the original example, I made some personal tweaks, light yellow background, rounded corners, drop shadow. This makes the tooltip feel more like a “modern web app” style. Key takeaway: opts_tooltip() accepts arbitrary CSS, which means with a little front-end knowledge, you can make the tooltip look however you want.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3: Programming Interactive Data Visualisation with R
text:
2.4 Displaying Statistics in the Tooltip
A more advanced trick, instead of showing raw data, the tooltip displays computed statistics. For example, showing the mean Maths score and 95% confidence interval for each race:

tooltip_stats <- function(y, ymax, accuracy = .01) {
  mean_val <- scales::number(y, accuracy = accuracy)
  sem <- scales::number(ymax - y, accuracy = accuracy)
  paste0("Mean Maths Score: ", mean_val, "\nStandard Error: ±", sem)
}

gg_summary <- ggplot(data = exam_data, 
                     aes(x = RACE)) +
  stat_summary(
    aes(y = MATHS, 
        tooltip = after_stat(tooltip_stats(y, ymax))),  
    fun.data = "mean_se", 
    geom = GeomInteractiveCol,  
    fill = "#5B9BD5",
    width = 0.6
  ) +
  stat_summary(
    aes(y = MATHS),
    fun.data = mean_se,
    geom = "errorbar", 
    width = 0.2, 
    linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  labs(x = "Race", y = "Maths Score",
       title = "Maths Score Comparison by Race (with Standard Error)") +
  theme_minimal()

girafe(ggobj = gg_summary,
       width_svg = 8,
       height_svg = 8 * 0.618)





My thoughts: This example made me realise that after_stat() is a really powerful tool, it allows us to reference computed values after ggplot has done the statistical calculation. This solves a core problem: the tooltip shows not raw data but values computed by the chart itself. If you wanted to achieve this manually, you’d have to group_by + summarise first, then plot much more cumbersome.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3: Programming Interactive Data Visualisation with R
text:
2.5 Hover Effect with data_id
tooltip is “look where you point” information display, while data_id is for linking and highlighting , all elements sharing the same data_id get highlighted together on hover:

p <- ggplot(data = exam_data, 
            aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(           
    aes(data_id = CLASS),     # Students from the same class highlight together
    stackgroups = TRUE,               
    binwidth = 1,                        
    method = "histodot") +               
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,               
                     breaks = NULL)

girafe(                                  
  ggobj = p,                             
  width_svg = 6,                         
  height_svg = 6 * 0.618                      
)                                        





My thoughts: This is the essence of data_id, it extends a single data point’s “individual identity” into a “group identity”. When analysing class-level performance, hovering over any student instantly reveals “where the rest of their classmates fall on the score range” far more intuitive than a static plot.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3: Programming Interactive Data Visualisation with R
text:
2.6 Styling the Hover Effect
The default highlight is orange (fill: orange). Through opts_hover() and opts_hover_inv(), we can fully control both the highlighted and “dimmed” styles:

p <- ggplot(data = exam_data, 
            aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(              
    aes(data_id = CLASS),              
    stackgroups = TRUE,                  
    binwidth = 1,                        
    method = "histodot") +               
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,               
                     breaks = NULL)

girafe(                                  
  ggobj = p,                             
  width_svg = 6,                         
  height_svg = 6 * 0.618,
  options = list(                        
    opts_hover(css = "fill: #C00000; stroke: black; stroke-width: 1.5px;"),  
    opts_hover_inv(css = "opacity: 0.15;")   # Non-selected elements fade out
  )                                        
)                                        





My thoughts: opts_hover_inv() is what I think is the most clever part, it defines “what non-highlighted elements should look like”. By dropping opacity to 0.15, unselected points almost “disappear”, and the visual impact of the highlighted group is amplified. This is the classic “focus + context” design, emphasising the focal point while preserving context.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3: Programming Interactive Data Visualisation with R
text:
2.7 Combining Tooltip and Hover
The two interactions can absolutely coexist. A common pairing: data_id for group highlighting, tooltip for showing specific content:

p <- ggplot(data = exam_data, 
            aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(              
    aes(tooltip = CLASS, 
        data_id = CLASS),              
    stackgroups = TRUE,                  
    binwidth = 1,                        
    method = "histodot") +               
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,               
                     breaks = NULL)

girafe(                                  
  ggobj = p,                             
  width_svg = 6,                         
  height_svg = 6 * 0.618,
  options = list(                        
    opts_hover(css = "fill: #202020;"),  
    opts_hover_inv(css = "opacity: 0.2;") 
  )                                        
)                                        





My thoughts: When tooltip and data_id share the same variable (CLASS), the experience feels most natural , “see all students in this class, and know which class it is”, that’s intuitive double-feedback.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3: Programming Interactive Data Visualisation with R
text:
2.8 Click-to-Navigate with onclick
onclick turns data points into “hyperlinks” , clicking jumps to a related page:

exam_data$onclick <- sprintf(
  "window.open(\"%s%s\")",
  "https://www.moe.gov.sg/schoolfinder?journey=Primary%20school",
  as.character(exam_data$ID))

p <- ggplot(data = exam_data, 
            aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(              
    aes(onclick = onclick),              
    stackgroups = TRUE,                  
    binwidth = 1,                        
    method = "histodot") +               
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,               
                     breaks = NULL)

girafe(                                  
  ggobj = p,                             
  width_svg = 6,                         
  height_svg = 6 * 0.618)                                        





My thoughts: onclick accepts arbitrary JavaScript code as a string, so theoretically you can do far more than just “open a new window”, trigger pop-ups, modify other page elements, submit forms, etc. However, there’s a pitfall here: if the string concatenated for the onclick field contains special characters (quotes, backslashes), it can easily cause JS errors. In production, it’s best to do a proper escape.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3: Programming Interactive Data Visualisation with R
text:
2.9 Coordinated Multiple Views
This is one of ggiraph’s most valuable features, two charts linked through a shared data_id:

p1 <- ggplot(data = exam_data, 
             aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(              
    aes(data_id = ID),              
    stackgroups = TRUE,                  
    binwidth = 1,                        
    method = "histodot") +  
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 100)) + 
  scale_y_continuous(NULL, breaks = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Maths Score Distribution")

p2 <- ggplot(data = exam_data, 
             aes(x = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(              
    aes(data_id = ID),              
    stackgroups = TRUE,                  
    binwidth = 1,                        
    method = "histodot") + 
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 100)) + 
  scale_y_continuous(NULL, breaks = NULL) +
  labs(title = "English Score Distribution")

girafe(code = print(p1 + p2),    # Use patchwork's + to combine the two plots
       width_svg = 8,
       height_svg = 4,
       options = list(
         opts_hover(css = "fill: #C00000;"),
         opts_hover_inv(css = "opacity: 0.2;")
       )
) 





My core reflection: This is the technique I find most “useful” in this entire assignment.

Looking at a single histogram, I can only know “the distribution of Maths scores”
But with linking added, hovering on the high-Maths region instantly reveals where these students sit on the English chart are they equally strong? Or are they unbalanced?
This kind of “cross-variable exploration” is something static charts simply cannot do

The key to making it work: both charts must use the same data_id (here, ID), otherwise ggiraph doesn’t know how to map between them.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3: Programming Interactive Data Visualisation with R
section: 3.1 Creating a Scatter Plot with plot_ly()
text:
3.1 Creating a Scatter Plot with plot_ly()

plot_ly(data = exam_data, 
        x = ~MATHS,
        y = ~ENGLISH)





My thoughts: The ~MATHS syntax confused me at first, why the ~? Then I understood: it’s R’s formula notation, telling plotly “this is a column name in the data, not a regular variable”. Once you get used to it, it’s quite concise.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3: Programming Interactive Data Visualisation with R
text:
3.2 Adding Colour Encoding

plot_ly(data = exam_data, 
        x = ~MATHS,
        y = ~ENGLISH,
        color = ~RACE,
        colors = "Set1")    # Use ColorBrewer's Set1 palette





My thoughts: There’s a “hidden feature” of plotly here, clicking on legend items toggles the visibility of corresponding categories. This is something static ggplot2 can never do. During data exploration, the ability to “filter out a category with one click and observe what’s left” is incredibly practical.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3: Programming Interactive Data Visualisation with R
text:
3.3 Converting a ggplot with ggplotly()

p <- ggplot(data = exam_data, 
            aes(x = MATHS, y = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = RACE), size = 2, alpha = 0.7) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 100), ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(title = "Maths vs English Scores",
       x = "Maths", y = "English") +
  theme_minimal()

ggplotly(p)





My thoughts and comparison:

plot_ly(): Independent syntax, requires learning a new system, but offers the best support for plotly’s native features
ggplotly(): Almost zero learning cost (sticks with ggplot syntax), but some complex ggplot features get “lost in translation”

Personally, I lean more towards ggplotly() because I’m already used to ggplot syntax, and in most cases “basic interactivity” is enough; we don’t need plotly’s full set of advanced features.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3: Programming Interactive Data Visualisation with R
text:
3.4 Coordinated Multiple Views with plotly
Linking with plotly takes three steps: use highlight_key() to create shared data → plot two charts → combine them with subplot().

shared_data <- highlight_key(exam_data)

p1 <- ggplot(shared_data, 
             aes(x = MATHS, y = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.6, color = "#5B9BD5") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 100), ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(title = "Maths vs English") +
  theme_minimal()

p2 <- ggplot(shared_data, 
             aes(x = MATHS, y = SCIENCE)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.6, color = "#ED7D31") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 100), ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(title = "Maths vs Science") +
  theme_minimal()

subplot(ggplotly(p1), 
        ggplotly(p2), 
        nrows = 1) %>%
  highlight(on = "plotly_selected",     # Triggered by box-select
            off = "plotly_doubleclick") # Cleared by double-click





My thoughts: plotly’s linking has one killer feature beyond ggiraph box select / lasso select. You can “draw a region” and the points inside get highlighted in the other chart. This is especially useful for exploring “doubly-high / doubly-low / unbalanced” students.
highlight_key() is essentially crosstalk::SharedData, it creates a “shared identity” object that lets multiple widgets know “this is the same batch of data”.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3: Programming Interactive Data Visualisation with R
text:
4.1 Interactive Tables with DT
First let’s see what DT produces on its own:

DT::datatable(
  exam_data %>% select(-tooltip, -onclick),  # Drop the helper columns we added earlier
  class = "compact",
  options = list(
    pageLength = 5,
    scrollX = TRUE
  ),
  caption = "Student Exam Results"
)





My thoughts: The search, sort, and pagination features DT provides are completely “out of the box”, backed by the JavaScript DataTables library. Functionality that would normally require lots of front-end code is achieved in R with a single line. This is the magic of the htmlwidgets ecosystem.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3: Programming Interactive Data Visualisation with R
section: 4.2 Linking a Scatter Plot with a Table
text:
4.2 Linking a Scatter Plot with a Table
Finally, a comprehensive example, linking a scatter plot and a table via crosstalk:

shared_exam <- highlight_key(exam_data %>% select(-tooltip, -onclick))

scatter <- ggplot(shared_exam, 
                  aes(x = MATHS, y = ENGLISH, color = RACE)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, alpha = 0.7) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 100), ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Box-select students on the scatter plot — the table below highlights in sync")

scatter_plotly <- ggplotly(scatter) %>%
  highlight(on = "plotly_selected", 
            off = "plotly_doubleclick")

table <- DT::datatable(shared_exam,
                       options = list(pageLength = 5))

# Use crosstalk::bscols to stack them vertically
crosstalk::bscols(
  widths = c(12, 12),
  scatter_plotly,
  table
)















My core reflection: This example made me truly understand the ultimate form of “interactive data visualisation”

Charts are no longer the presentation of conclusions, but the entry point of exploration.

The reader can “circle a region of interesting points on the chart → instantly see their detailed information in the table”. This kind of usage transforms the reader’s role from “receiver” into “researcher”.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3: Programming Interactive Data Visualisation with R
section: 5.2 The Core Idea I Took Away
text:
5.2 The Core Idea I Took Away
Interactivity isn’t “decoration” — it’s an “expansion of information density”. A static chart can only present information from one fixed perspective, while an interactive chart lets readers dynamically switch perspectives based on their interests, which essentially turns “one chart” into “infinitely many charts”.
But it’s also important to recognise that more interactivity isn’t always better:

If a chart’s core conclusion is already crystal clear (e.g. “this metric has been declining year-on-year for the past decade”), adding interactivity actually distracts
The scenarios truly suited for interactivity are: multivariate exploration, individual-level lookups, and analyses that need “filter then re-observe”

title: Hands-on Exercise 3: Programming Interactive Data Visualisation with R
text:
5.3 Pitfalls I Encountered

girafe() measures dimensions in inches, not pixels. I initially set width_svg = 600 and the chart blew up the page.
ggplotly() cannot perfectly convert all ggplot elements. For instance, facet_wrap titles sometimes get distorted. For complex ggplot charts, finalise the static version first, then convert.
crosstalk::bscols requires Bootstrap dependencies, first run may prompt package installation.
When concatenating JS strings for the onclick field, sprintf() is safer than paste0() because it gives more precise control over quote escaping.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5: Visualising Multivariate Data
text:
Welcome to my fifth hands-on exercise. This time the focus is squarely on multivariate data, which is what most real datasets look like once we stop pretending the world has only two dimensions. Across the five sections below, I work through five complementary techniques, each suited to a slightly different analytical question:

Ternary plots for three-part compositional data (Chapter 13).
Correlation visualisation for pairwise relationships among many numerical variables (Chapter 6).
Heatmaps for spotting clusters and patterns across an entire matrix at once (Chapter 14).
Parallel coordinates plots for tracing how individual observations behave across many variables (Chapter 15).
Treemaps for hierarchical part-to-whole composition (Chapter 16).

title: Hands-on Exercise 5: Visualising Multivariate Data
section: 2.1 What is a ternary plot, intuitively?
text:
2.1 What is a ternary plot, intuitively?
A ternary plot is a triangle in which every point inside represents a three-part composition that sums to 100%. Each side of the triangle is one component, and the position of the point tells me how that observation splits between the three. The classic textbook example is soil composition (sand, silt, clay), but here I use it for Singapore’s population structure: young, economically active, and old.
The reason a ternary plot beats three separate bar charts is that the three proportions are constrained: if young goes up, one of the others must come down. The triangle visualises that trade-off directly.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5: Visualising Multivariate Data
text:
2.2 Setting up the packages

pacman::p_load(plotly, ggtern, tidyverse)

title: Hands-on Exercise 5: Visualising Multivariate Data
text:
2.3 Importing and preparing the data

pop_data <- read_csv("data/respopagsex2000to2018_tidy.csv")

The raw data has age groups in long format, but for a ternary plot I need exactly three numbers per row. So I bucket the age groups into YOUNG, ACTIVE, and OLD, then keep only 2018.

agpop_mutated <- pop_data %>%
  mutate(`Year` = as.character(Year)) %>%
  spread(AG, Population) %>%
  mutate(YOUNG = rowSums(.[4:8])) %>%
  mutate(ACTIVE = rowSums(.[9:16])) %>%
  mutate(OLD = rowSums(.[17:21])) %>%
  mutate(TOTAL = rowSums(.[22:24])) %>%
  filter(Year == 2018) %>%
  filter(TOTAL > 0)

What is actually happening here:

spread() pivots age groups from rows to columns so I can sum them by category.
rowSums(.[4:8]) is a compact way to add specific columns by position. It works, but it is fragile if column order ever changes, so in production code I would probably use select() plus column names instead.
The final filter(TOTAL > 0) removes subzones with no residents, which would otherwise be undefined on the triangle.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5: Visualising Multivariate Data
text:
2.4 Building a static ternary plot

ggtern(data = agpop_mutated, 
       aes(x = YOUNG, y = ACTIVE, z = OLD)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Population structure, 2018") +
  theme_rgbw()

theme_rgbw() gives the triangle a clean white background with light gridlines, which I find much easier to read than the default. The ggtern API uses x, y, and z instead of two axes, but otherwise everything composes like normal ggplot layers.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5: Visualising Multivariate Data
text:
2.5 Building an interactive ternary plot
For the interactive version I switch to plot_ly() with type = "scatterternary". The interactivity is genuinely useful here because each point is a planning subzone, and being able to hover to identify which subzone has an unusually old or young profile is much more efficient than reading a legend.

label <- function(txt) {
  list(
    text = txt, 
    x = 0.1, y = 1,
    ax = 0, ay = 0,
    xref = "paper", yref = "paper", 
    align = "center",
    font = list(family = "serif", size = 15, color = "white"),
    bgcolor = "#b3b3b3", bordercolor = "black", borderwidth = 2
  )
}

axis <- function(txt) {
  list(
    title = txt, tickformat = ".0%", tickfont = list(size = 10)
  )
}

ternaryAxes <- list(
  aaxis = axis("Young"), 
  baxis = axis("Active"), 
  caxis = axis("Old")
)

plot_ly(
  agpop_mutated, 
  a = ~YOUNG, 
  b = ~ACTIVE, 
  c = ~OLD, 
  color = I("black"), 
  type = "scatterternary"
) %>%
  layout(
    annotations = label("Ternary Markers"), 
    ternary = ternaryAxes
  )

title: Hands-on Exercise 5: Visualising Multivariate Data
text:
2.6 My takeaway
Ternary plots are surprisingly powerful when the data really is compositional. And They only make sense when the three parts logically sum to a whole. For Singapore’s age structure, the cluster of points pulled towards the “active” corner tells the demographic story in one glance.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5: Visualising Multivariate Data
text:
3.1 Why bother visualising correlations?
When I have ten or more numerical variables, eyeballing a correlation table of numbers is exhausting and error-prone. A visual correlation matrix solves three problems at once:

It reveals the pairwise relationships between variables at a glance.
It feeds into downstream analyses such as regression and factor analysis.
It acts as a diagnostic for multicollinearity before I run any model.

For this section I use the Wine Quality dataset, with 11 numerical chemical properties across roughly 6,500 wines.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5: Visualising Multivariate Data
text:
3.2 Packages

pacman::p_load(corrplot, ggstatsplot, tidyverse)

title: Hands-on Exercise 5: Visualising Multivariate Data
text:
3.3 Importing the data

wine <- read_csv("data/wine_quality.csv")

title: Hands-on Exercise 5: Visualising Multivariate Data
text:
3.4 Method 1: Base R pairs()
The simplest scatterplot matrix uses base R’s pairs():

pairs(wine[, 2:12])

Since a correlation matrix is symmetric, showing both halves is redundant. I prefer to show only the lower half:

pairs(wine[, 2:12], upper.panel = NULL)

And to be smarter still, I can replace one half with the actual correlation coefficients, sized by magnitude:

panel.cor <- function(x, y, digits = 2, prefix = "", cex.cor, ...) {
  usr <- par("usr")
  on.exit(par(usr))
  par(usr = c(0, 1, 0, 1))
  r <- abs(cor(x, y, use = "complete.obs"))
  txt <- format(c(r, 0.123456789), digits = digits)[1]
  txt <- paste(prefix, txt, sep = "")
  if (missing(cex.cor)) cex.cor <- 0.8 / strwidth(txt)
  text(0.5, 0.5, txt, cex = cex.cor * (1 + r) / 2)
}

pairs(wine[, 2:12], upper.panel = panel.cor)







NoteWhen pairs() breaks down



With 6,500 observations the scatter clouds become huge inky blobs and stop being readable. That is exactly the limitation that motivates the corrgram approach below.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5: Visualising Multivariate Data
text:
3.5 Method 2: ggcorrmat() from ggstatsplot
ggstatsplot::ggcorrmat() is my favourite for reporting, because it produces a publication-ready figure with statistical annotation baked in:

ggstatsplot::ggcorrmat(
  data = wine, 
  cor.vars = 1:11,
  ggcorrplot.args = list(outline.color = "black", 
                         hc.order = TRUE,
                         tl.cex = 10),
  title = "Correlogram for wine dataset",
  subtitle = "Four pairs are not significant at p < 0.05"
)

hc.order = TRUE reorders the variables by hierarchical clustering, similar variables end up next to each other, so the block structure of the correlation matrix becomes visually obvious.
For grouped comparisons (red wine vs white wine), I can use grouped_ggcorrmat():

grouped_ggcorrmat(
  data = wine,
  cor.vars = 1:11,
  grouping.var = type,
  type = "robust",
  p.adjust.method = "holm",
  plotgrid.args = list(ncol = 2),
  ggcorrplot.args = list(outline.color = "black", 
                         hc.order = TRUE,
                         tl.cex = 10),
  annotation.args = list(
    tag_levels = "a",
    title = "Correlogram for wine dataset",
    caption = "Dataset: UCI Machine Learning Repository"
  )
)

title: Hands-on Exercise 5: Visualising Multivariate Data
text:
3.6 Method 3: corrplot for fine control
Where ggcorrmat is opinionated, corrplot is endlessly customisable. First I compute the correlation matrix explicitly:

wine.cor <- cor(wine[, 1:11])
corrplot(wine.cor)

The default uses circles, with blue for positive and red for negative correlations, and colour intensity for magnitude.

3.6.1 Changing the visual encoding
Seven method options exist (circle, square, ellipse, number, shade, color, pie). Ellipses are my go-to because the tilt of the ellipse encodes the sign of the correlation visually:

corrplot(wine.cor, 
         method = "ellipse",
         type = "lower",
         diag = FALSE,
         tl.col = "black")



3.6.2 Mixed layout: glyphs on one side, numbers on the other
This is the design I usually settle on for final reports because it captures both shape and exact magnitude in one figure:

corrplot.mixed(wine.cor, 
               lower = "ellipse", 
               upper = "number",
               tl.pos = "lt",
               diag = "l",
               tl.col = "black")



3.6.3 Significance testing overlay
Correlation strength is not the whole story.

wine.sig = cor.mtest(wine.cor, conf.level = .95)

corrplot(wine.cor,
         method = "number",
         type = "lower",
         diag = FALSE,
         tl.col = "black",
         tl.srt = 45,
         p.mat = wine.sig$p,
         sig.level = .05)

Non-significant cells get crossed out, which is much more informative than presenting raw r-values as if they were all equally trustworthy.


3.6.4 Reordering with hierarchical clustering
Reordering is where corrgrams really earn their keep. By default the variables appear in whatever order the dataframe had them, which is rarely the most informative arrangement:

corrplot(wine.cor, 
         method = "ellipse", 
         tl.pos = "lt",
         tl.col = "black",
         order = "hclust",
         hclust.method = "ward.D",
         addrect = 3)

The addrect = 3 argument draws boxes around three clusters.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5: Visualising Multivariate Data
text:
3.7 My takeaway
For exploration I reach for corrplot because of its flexibility. For formal reports I prefer ggcorrmat because the statistical annotation is built in. Either way, reordering by clustering is the single most underrated technique here, it transforms a chaotic matrix into a structured one.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5: Visualising Multivariate Data
text:
4.1 What heatmaps are good at
A heatmap is essentially a coloured table. Rows are observations, columns are variables, and each cell’s colour encodes a value. The reason this works so well is that human vision is very good at picking out horizontal bands of similar colour (similar observations) and vertical bands (related variables). Adding dendrograms on the sides lets the algorithm reorder both axes so those bands actually emerge.
For this section I use the World Happiness 2018 dataset.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5: Visualising Multivariate Data
text:
4.2 Packages

pacman::p_load(seriation, dendextend, heatmaply, tidyverse)

title: Hands-on Exercise 5: Visualising Multivariate Data
text:
4.3 Importing and preparing the data

wh <- read_csv("data/WHData-2018.csv")
row.names(wh) <- wh$Country

Setting row names to country names is essential, otherwise the heatmap labels are useless row numbers. The next step is converting to a matrix because most heatmap functions require that input class:

wh_matrix <- data.matrix(wh)

title: Hands-on Exercise 5: Visualising Multivariate Data
text:
4.4 Static heatmap with heatmap()
The base R heatmap() is a fine starting point:

wh_heatmap <- heatmap(wh_matrix,
                      Rowv = NA, Colv = NA)

With Rowv = NA and Colv = NA, both dendrograms are switched off, so I see the raw matrix with no reordering. That is rarely what I want, but it is useful as a baseline.

4.4.1 The scaling problem
If I plot the matrix without scaling, one variable (Happiness Score) dominates because its raw values are much larger than the others. Everything else looks washed out. Column-wise scaling fixes this:

wh_heatmap <- heatmap(wh_matrix,
                      scale = "column",
                      cexRow = 0.6, 
                      cexCol = 0.8,
                      margins = c(10, 4))

scale = "column" z-scores each column, so every variable now contributes on equal footing. This is a small change with an enormous effect on interpretability.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5: Visualising Multivariate Data
text:
4.5 Interactive heatmap with heatmaply
heatmaply produces interactive heatmaps that render as standalone HTML.

heatmaply(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)])


4.5.1 Three data transformation methods
heatmaply offers three transformations, and choosing between them is more than cosmetic:

# Scaling: assumes (or imposes) normal-like distributions
heatmaply(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)],
          scale = "column")

# Normalising: maps to [0, 1] using min and max
heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]))

# Percentising: maps each value to its empirical percentile
heatmaply(percentize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]))


Scale when variables are roughly normal and outliers are meaningful.
Normalise when distributions are skewed but I still want raw shape preserved.
Percentise when I care about relative rank rather than absolute values, which is often the case for indicators across countries.



4.5.2 Picking the right clustering setup
Choosing a clustering method by intuition feels arbitrary. The dendextend package lets me pick statistically:

wh_d <- dist(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]), method = "euclidean")
dend_expend(wh_d)[[3]]

The output table shows an optim score for each clustering method. The highest score wins, which in this dataset is average. Then I find the best number of clusters:

wh_clust <- hclust(wh_d, method = "average")
num_k <- find_k(wh_clust)
plot(num_k)

Putting both choices into the heatmap call:

heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]),
          dist_method = "euclidean",
          hclust_method = "average",
          k_row = 3)



4.5.3 Seriation: getting the row order right
Clustering tells me the tree structure, but it does not tell me how to rotate the branches. Two valid orderings of the same cluster tree can produce very different-looking heatmaps. The seriate = "OLO" (Optimal Leaf Ordering) argument fixes this by minimising the sum of dissimilarities between adjacent rows:

heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]),
          seriate = "OLO")



4.5.4 Final polished version
Putting it all together with thoughtful styling:

heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]),
          Colv = NA,
          seriate = "none",
          colors = Blues,
          k_row = 5,
          margins = c(NA, 200, 60, NA),
          fontsize_row = 4,
          fontsize_col = 5,
          main = "World Happiness Score and Variables by Country, 2018",
          xlab = "World Happiness Indicators",
          ylab = "World Countries")

title: Hands-on Exercise 5: Visualising Multivariate Data
text:
4.6 My takeaway
Heatmaps reward attention to three details: scaling, clustering choice, and leaf ordering. Get all three right and the patterns essentially announce themselves. Get any one wrong and the chart can mislead.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5: Visualising Multivariate Data
section: 5.1 What parallel coordinates plots do differently
text:
5.1 What parallel coordinates plots do differently
If a scatterplot matrix shows me pairwise relationships, a parallel coordinates plot shows me whole observations as lines across many variables. Each vertical axis is one variable. Each line is one observation, threading through all the variables in sequence. This is uniquely good at:

Identifying clusters of similarly-behaved observations.
Spotting outliers that take an unusual path across variables.
Characterising customer segments or country groupings.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5: Visualising Multivariate Data
text:
5.2 Packages

pacman::p_load(GGally, parallelPlot, tidyverse)

title: Hands-on Exercise 5: Visualising Multivariate Data
text:
5.3 Importing the data

wh <- read_csv("data/WHData-2018.csv")

title: Hands-on Exercise 5: Visualising Multivariate Data
text:
5.4 Static plot with ggparcoord()
A bare-minimum plot:

ggparcoord(data = wh, 
           columns = c(7:12))

This is honestly not very useful on its own. Without colour or scaling, all lines pile on top of each other. The makeover below is where it becomes informative:

ggparcoord(data = wh, 
           columns = c(7:12), 
           groupColumn = 2,
           scale = "uniminmax",
           alphaLines = 0.2,
           boxplot = TRUE, 
           title = "Parallel Coordinates Plot of World Happiness Variables")

The four arguments that transform this chart:

groupColumn = 2 colours lines by Region, which is where regional patterns start to emerge.
scale = "uniminmax" puts every axis on a 0-to-1 range, so axes are comparable.
alphaLines = 0.2 makes lines semi-transparent, so overlapping bundles look denser. This is essential for any dataset above maybe 30 observations.
boxplot = TRUE overlays a boxplot per axis, summarising distribution shape.


5.4.1 Faceting by region
For comparing regions head-to-head, faceting works beautifully:

ggparcoord(data = wh, 
           columns = c(7:12), 
           groupColumn = 2,
           scale = "uniminmax",
           alphaLines = 0.2,
           boxplot = TRUE, 
           title = "Parallel Coordinates by Region") +
  facet_wrap(~ Region) + 
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))

The angle = 30, hjust = 1 combination rotates and right-aligns axis labels so they do not overlap the plot, which is a small detail that makes a big visual difference.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5: Visualising Multivariate Data
text:
5.5 Interactive plot with parallelPlot
For exploratory work, interactivity is genuinely useful here because clicking on an axis recolours all lines by that variable, which is the fastest way to ask “what drives this variable?”:

wh <- wh %>%
  select("Happiness score", c(7:12))

parallelPlot(wh,
             rotateTitle = TRUE)


5.5.1 Customising colour and adding histograms

parallelPlot(wh,
             continuousCS = "YlOrRd",
             rotateTitle = TRUE)

histoVisibility <- rep(TRUE, ncol(wh))
parallelPlot(wh,
             rotateTitle = TRUE,
             histoVisibility = histoVisibility)

The histograms along each axis are an underrated feature, because they show me the marginal distribution of each variable without leaving the chart.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5: Visualising Multivariate Data
text:
5.6 My takeaway
Parallel coordinates plots have a steep aesthetic learning curve. The defaults look terrible. But once I add scaling, transparency, grouping colour, and boxplots, they become one of the most informative views possible for medium-sized multivariate datasets. The interactive version is what I would actually use in a live exploratory session.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5: Visualising Multivariate Data
text:
6.1 When to use a treemap
Treemaps shine for hierarchical part-to-whole data where I care about both the level of the hierarchy and the relative sizes of leaves. Classic use cases:

Budget breakdowns by department and team.
Stock market sectors and constituent companies.
Property transactions by region, planning area, and project (which is exactly what I do here).

The two things I will always encode are rectangle size (a magnitude) and rectangle colour (a separate metric, often a rate or median).

title: Hands-on Exercise 5: Visualising Multivariate Data
text:
6.2 Packages

pacman::p_load(treemap, treemapify, tidyverse)

title: Hands-on Exercise 5: Visualising Multivariate Data
text:
6.3 Data wrangling
The raw REALIS 2018 dataset is at the transaction level. A treemap needs aggregated values, so I group and summarise:

realis2018 <- read_csv("data/realis2018.csv")

realis2018_summarised <- realis2018 %>% 
  group_by(`Project Name`, `Planning Region`, 
           `Planning Area`, `Property Type`, 
           `Type of Sale`) %>%
  summarise(`Total Unit Sold` = sum(`No. of Units`, na.rm = TRUE), 
            `Total Area` = sum(`Area (sqm)`, na.rm = TRUE),
            `Median Unit Price ($ psm)` = median(`Unit Price ($ psm)`, na.rm = TRUE),
            `Median Transacted Price` = median(`Transacted Price ($)`, na.rm = TRUE))

Notice the pipe pattern: group, then summarise. This is one of those dplyr workflows that you internalise once and then use forever. The na.rm = TRUE is essential because any missing value in a column would otherwise propagate to the whole summary.
Filter to a single property type and sale type to keep the example focused:

realis2018_selected <- realis2018_summarised %>%
  filter(`Property Type` == "Condominium", 
         `Type of Sale` == "Resale")

title: Hands-on Exercise 5: Visualising Multivariate Data
text:
6.4 Static treemap with treemap()
The three arguments that do most of the work are index, vSize, and vColor:

treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index = c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize = "Total Unit Sold",
        vColor = "Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        title = "Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2018",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)")







WarningA subtle gotcha



By default, vColor does not actually map to a colour gradient. Without setting type, treemap() assumes type = "index" and colours rectangles by hierarchy category instead of by the numeric variable.



6.4.1 Fixing the colour mapping
To actually map colour to the numeric variable, I need to set type:

treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index = c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize = "Total Unit Sold",
        vColor = "Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        type = "value",
        title = "Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2018",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)")



6.4.2 “value” vs “manual”: what is the difference?
This tripped me up at first. Both use vColor, but the mapping logic differs:

type = "value" treats the palette as diverging around zero. Negative values pull towards the left-end colour, positive values pull towards the right. Good for data that can be negative.
type = "manual" maps min(values) to the left end and max(values) to the right end, with mean in the middle. Good for strictly-positive data.

For unit prices, which are all positive, manual with a sequential palette like Blues is the right combination:

treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index = c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize = "Total Unit Sold",
        vColor = "Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        type = "manual",
        palette = "Blues", 
        title = "Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2018",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)")



6.4.3 Layout algorithms
treemap supports two algorithms:

squarified: optimises aspect ratios so rectangles are close to squares. Ignores sort order.
pivotSize (default): respects a sortID ordering at the cost of slightly worse aspect ratios.


treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index = c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize = "Total Unit Sold",
        vColor = "Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        type = "manual",
        palette = "Blues", 
        algorithm = "pivotSize",
        sortID = "Median Transacted Price",
        title = "Sorted by Median Transacted Price")

I usually pick squarified for purely visual comparison and pivotSize with sortID when there is a meaningful order to encode.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5: Visualising Multivariate Data
text:
6.5 Treemap with treemapify (ggplot grammar)
treemapify lets me build treemaps inside ggplot, which is great when I want to combine with other ggplot features:

ggplot(data = realis2018_selected, 
       aes(area = `Total Unit Sold`,
           fill = `Median Unit Price ($ psm)`,
           subgroup = `Planning Region`,
           subgroup2 = `Planning Area`)) + 
  geom_treemap() +
  geom_treemap_subgroup2_border(colour = "gray40", size = 2) +
  geom_treemap_subgroup_border(colour = "gray20")

The two *_border layers draw nested borders for each hierarchy level, which makes the structure visually obvious. I find this version cleaner than the treemap() output for final reports.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5: Visualising Multivariate Data
text:
6.6 Interactive treemap with d3treeR
For drilldown exploration, the interactive d3treeR package wraps a treemap object into a clickable d3 visualisation:

# install.packages("devtools")
# library(devtools)
# install_github("timelyportfolio/d3treeR")
library(d3treeR)


tm <- treemap(realis2018_summarised,
        index = c("Planning Region", "Planning Area"),
        vSize = "Total Unit Sold",
        vColor = "Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        type = "value",
        title = "Private Residential Property Sold, 2018",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)")

d3tree(tm, rootname = "Singapore")

Clicking a region zooms into that region’s planning areas. For a stakeholder-facing dashboard this is genuinely useful, because it lets the viewer explore at their own pace instead of forcing one fixed view.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5: Visualising Multivariate Data
text:
6.7 My takeaway
Treemaps are easy to make wrong and reasonably easy to make right. The two non-negotiables are: (1) set type explicitly so colour actually maps to your numeric variable, and (2) use a sequential palette when values are strictly positive. Everything else is polish.

title: Hands-on Exercise 7: Visualising and Analysing Time-oriented Data
text:
Time-oriented data is everywhere in the kind of problems this course keeps coming back to: server logs, visitor arrivals, crop yields, sales records. The hard part is that a plain line chart often hides as much as it shows once the series gets long or once I want to compare many series at once. In this exercise I practise three families of techniques that each attack a different weakness of the line chart:

a calendar heatmap, which lays out a long event log on a weekday by hour grid so that daily and weekly rhythms jump out,
a cycle plot, which separates the within-year seasonal shape from the long-run trend, and
a slopegraph, which strips a before-and-after comparison down to the slope of each line.

My goal here is not just to reproduce the plots but to understand which question each chart form is actually good at answering.


I load every package this exercise relies on in a single pacman::p_load() call. This is my standard loader because it installs anything missing and then attaches everything in one line, which keeps the setup chunk tidy.


Show the code
pacman::p_load(scales, viridis, lubridate, ggthemes,
               gridExtra, readxl, knitr, data.table,
               tidyverse)


A quick note on what each one does in this exercise: lubridate and base R give me the date and time parsing, data.table speeds up the row-wise field derivation, ggthemes supplies the clean theme_tufte() look, and scales formats the percentage labels. tidyverse is doing the heavy lifting throughout for wrangling and plotting, including the slopegraph near the end, which I build with ggplot2 directly.






NoteA note on the slopegraph package



The brief draws its slopegraph with newggslopegraph() from CGPfunctions. That package was archived from CRAN in November 2025, and its GitHub version depends on ggmosaic, which is also unavailable for R 4.5, so neither a CRAN nor a GitHub install succeeds on a current setup. Rather than fight that dependency chain, I build the slopegraph from base ggplot2 later on. It is a little more code, but it removes a fragile dependency entirely.

The frame has three columns. timestamp stores the date-time in POSIXct form, source_country is the ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country code of the attack source, and tz is the time zone of the source IP address. The tz column is the detail that matters most, because the same instant in UTC means a different local weekday and hour depending on where the attacker sits, and the whole point of this chart is to read activity by local time of day.

title: Hands-on Exercise 7: Visualising and Analysing Time-oriented Data
text:
2.4 Data preparation

2.4.1 Deriving the weekday and hour fields
To plot a weekday by hour grid I first need a wkday field and an hour field. The tricky requirement is that both must be computed in the source’s own time zone, not mine. I wrap that logic in a small function so it can be applied one time-zone group at a time.


Show the code
make_hr_wkday <- function(ts, sc, tz) {
  real_times <- ymd_hms(ts,
                        tz = tz[1],
                        quiet = TRUE)
  wkday_en <- c("Sunday", "Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday",
                "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday")
  dt <- data.table(source_country = sc,
                   wkday = wkday_en[wday(real_times)],
                   hour = hour(real_times))
  return(dt)
}


Here ymd_hms() parses the timestamp into the time zone passed in, and hour() extracts the hour. For the weekday I deliberately avoid base R’s weekdays(). Instead I take the numeric weekday from wday(), where 1 is Sunday through 7 is Saturday, and index into a fixed English vector. I take tz[1] because the function receives one time zone per call, so every element of that vector is identical and I only need the first.






WarningWhy not weekdays(): a locale trap



The brief uses weekdays(real_times), which returns the day name in the system locale. On an English machine that gives “Monday”, “Tuesday”, and so on, exactly what wkday_levels expects. My Windows install runs in a non-English locale, so weekdays() hands back localised day names instead. None of those match the English entries in wkday_levels, so factor() turns every weekday into NA, na.omit() then drops every single row, and the faceted heatmap fails with “Faceting variables must have at least one value”. Deriving the weekday from the numeric wday() and mapping to fixed English names sidesteps the locale completely, so the same code behaves identically on any machine.








NoteWhy a custom function at all



ymd_hms() only accepts one time zone per call. Since the data spans many zones, I cannot convert the whole column in one shot. The clean fix is to split the data by tz and run this function within each group, which is what the next step does.




2.4.2 Building the attacks tibble
I set the weekday order myself so that the finished plot reads from Sunday at the bottom to Saturday at the top, then I apply the function group by group and lock both new fields into ordered factors.


Show the code
wkday_levels <- c('Saturday', 'Friday',
                  'Thursday', 'Wednesday',
                  'Tuesday', 'Monday',
                  'Sunday')

attacks <- attacks %>%
  group_by(tz) %>%
  do(make_hr_wkday(.$timestamp,
                   .$source_country,
                   .$tz)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(wkday = factor(
    wkday, levels = wkday_levels),
    hour  = factor(
      hour, levels = 0:23))

title: Hands-on Exercise 7: Visualising and Analysing Time-oriented Data
text:
2.5 Building the calendar heatmap
Now I aggregate to one count per weekday and hour, drop any missing combinations, and draw the grid.


Show the code
grouped <- attacks %>%
  count(wkday, hour) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  na.omit()

ggplot(grouped,
       aes(hour,
           wkday,
           fill = n)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white",
            linewidth = 0.1) +
  theme_tufte(base_family = "Helvetica") +
  coord_equal() +
  scale_fill_gradient(name = "# of attacks",
                      low = "sky blue",
                      high = "dark blue") +
  labs(x = NULL,
       y = NULL,
       title = "Attacks by weekday and time of day") +
  theme(axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
        legend.title = element_text(size = 8),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 6))









Walking through the choices I made: count() builds the n field that maps to fill, na.omit() removes rows where the time zone could not be parsed, and geom_tile() draws one rectangle per cell with a thin white border so the grid stays readable. theme_tufte() removes the chart junk that would otherwise compete with the colour signal, and coord_equal() keeps the cells square so no row or column looks artificially heavier. scale_fill_gradient() runs from light to dark blue so that darker simply means more attacks.






WarningA version gotcha I hit



The course code uses size = 0.1 inside geom_tile(). From ggplot2 3.4.0 onward the border thickness argument for tiles and lines was renamed to linewidth, and size now throws a deprecation warning. I switched to linewidth = 0.1 so the chunk runs cleanly on a current install. The visual is identical.

title: Hands-on Exercise 7: Visualising and Analysing Time-oriented Data
text:
2.6 Building multiple calendar heatmaps
A single grid mixes every country together. To compare patterns across the heaviest sources I rebuild the same chart faceted by country, focusing on the top four.

2.6.1 Deriving the attacks-by-country object


Show the code
attacks_by_country <- count(
  attacks, source_country) %>%
  mutate(percent = percent(n/sum(n))) %>%
  arrange(desc(n))


I count attacks per country, convert each count into a share of the total with percent(), and sort so the busiest countries sit at the top. The arrange() is what lets me grab the leaders by position in the next step.


2.6.2 Preparing the tidy data frame


Show the code
top4 <- attacks_by_country$source_country[1:4]
top4_attacks <- attacks %>%
  filter(source_country %in% top4) %>%
  count(source_country, wkday, hour) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(source_country = factor(
    source_country, levels = top4)) %>%
  na.omit()


I pull the four leading codes, keep only their records, and recompute the weekday-hour counts within each country. Setting source_country as a factor with levels = top4 means the four panels appear in descending order of attack volume rather than alphabetical order, which makes the facets easier to compare.


2.6.3 Plotting the multiple calendar heatmaps


Show the code
ggplot(top4_attacks,
       aes(hour,
           wkday,
           fill = n)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white",
            linewidth = 0.1) +
  theme_tufte(base_family = "Helvetica") +
  coord_equal() +
  scale_fill_gradient(name = "# of attacks",
                      low = "sky blue",
                      high = "dark blue") +
  facet_wrap(~source_country, ncol = 2) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL,
       title = "Attacks on top 4 countries by weekday and time of day") +
  theme(axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x = element_text(size = 7),
        plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
        legend.title = element_text(size = 8),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 6))









The only structural change from the single heatmap is facet_wrap(~source_country, ncol = 2), which repeats the grid once per country on a shared colour scale. The shared scale is important: because every panel reads against the same legend, I can compare absolute intensity across countries and not just the shape within each one.






NoteMy takeaway on calendar heatmaps



This chart form is at its best when I want to spot a rhythm in a high-volume log and I do not need exact numbers. The faceted version trades a little resolution for a direct visual comparison across groups. The whole exercise also reminded me that the local time zone, not UTC, is what makes the time-of-day pattern meaningful.

Show the code

                    levels = 1:12,
                    labels = month.abb,
                    ordered = TRUE)
air$year <- year(ymd(air$`Month-Year`))

3.3 Extracting the target country


Show the code
Vietnam <- air %>%
  select(`Vietnam`,
         month,
         year) %>%

I keep only Vietnam’s arrivals plus the month and year keys, and I restrict to 2010 onward so the cycle plot covers a clean recent decade.

title: Hands-on Exercise 7: Visualising and Analysing Time-oriented Data
section: 3.4 Computing the year-average arrivals by month
text:
3.4 Computing the year-average arrivals by month


Show the code
hline.data <- Vietnam %>%
  group_by(month) %>%
  summarise(avgvalue = mean(`Vietnam`))


This small summary holds one average per month. It becomes the reference line in each panel, which is the device that lets me read whether a given month sits above or below its own typical level.

title: Hands-on Exercise 7: Visualising and Analysing Time-oriented Data
text:
3.5 Plotting the cycle plot


Show the code
ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = Vietnam,
            aes(x = year,
                y = `Vietnam`,
                group = month),
            colour = "black") +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = avgvalue),
             data = hline.data,
             linetype = 6,
             colour = "red",
             linewidth = 0.5) +
  facet_grid(~month) +
  labs(title = "Visitor arrivals from Vietnam by air, Jan 2010-Dec 2019") +
  xlab("") +
  ylab("No. of Visitors") +
  theme_tufte(base_family = "Helvetica") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank())









The construction is two layers over a faceted canvas. The black geom_line() draws the trend across years within each month, grouped by month so the lines do not jump across panels. The red dashed geom_hline() pulls the per-month average from hline.data, giving each panel its own benchmark. facet_grid(~month) lays the twelve panels side by side so the eye sweeps across the seasonal shape from left to right while still seeing each month’s year-on-year movement.






WarningA subtle bug I corrected



The reference code put axis.text.x = element_blank() inside labs(). That argument is meaningless to labs(), so it silently does nothing and the year ticks stay on screen, which clutters twelve narrow panels. The correct home for it is theme(), so I moved it there. I also updated the geom_hline() thickness from size to linewidth for the same deprecation reason as before.








NoteMy takeaway on cycle plots



Reading this chart, the within-panel slope tells me the trend and the height of each panel relative to its red line tells me the seasonality. That separation is the whole value of the form. A single line chart of the same data would blend the two effects together and force me to guess which is which.

text:
4.1 Data import


Show the code
rice <- read_csv("data/rice.csv")

title: Hands-on Exercise 7: Visualising and Analysing Time-oriented Data
text:
4.2 Plotting the slopegraph
newggslopegraph() would normally do this in one call, but since I am avoiding that package I assemble the same Tufte-style slopegraph from ggplot2 layers. I keep the two endpoint years, turn Year into a two-level factor so it becomes two discrete columns, and draw one line per country with its name and value labelled on each side.


Show the code
rice_slope <- rice %>%
  filter(Year %in% c(1961, 1980)) %>%
  mutate(Year = factor(Year, levels = c("1961", "1980")))

ggplot(rice_slope, aes(x = Year, y = Yield, group = Country)) +
  geom_line(aes(colour = Country), linewidth = 1, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = Country), size = 2.5) +
  geom_text(data = filter(rice_slope, Year == "1961"),
            aes(label = sprintf("%s  %.1f", Country, Yield)),
            hjust = 1, nudge_x = -0.05, size = 3) +
  geom_text(data = filter(rice_slope, Year == "1980"),
            aes(label = sprintf("%.1f  %s", Yield, Country)),
            hjust = 0, nudge_x = 0.05, size = 3) +
  scale_x_discrete(position = "top",
                   expand = expansion(mult = 0.35)) +
  guides(colour = "none") +
  labs(title = "Rice Yield of Top 11 Asian Countries",
       subtitle = "1961-1980",
       x = NULL, y = NULL,
       caption = "Prepared by: Meng Tingyu") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
        axis.text.y = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5))









The structure is straightforward once the year is a factor. geom_line() and geom_point() draw the slope for each country, the two geom_text() layers place the country and its yield on the left and right edges, and scale_x_discrete(position = "top") with a wide expand keeps the year labels at the top while leaving room for the side text. Hiding the colour legend, the y-axis, and the gridlines is what gives the chart its minimal Tufte feel.






TipWhy factor the year



A slopegraph needs exactly two discrete columns. Leaving Year numeric would place the points on a continuous scale, and the spacing would no longer read as two clean snapshots. Forcing it to a factor with two levels is what gives the chart its two-column structure, the same factor-as-layout idea that fixed the heatmap axis order.








NoteMy takeaway on slopegraphs



The strength here is also the limitation. By showing only two time points the chart makes the ranking and the change instantly legible, but it throws away everything that happened in between. I would reach for this when the before-and-after comparison is the entire story, and reach for a cycle plot or line chart when the path matters.
